label: Enron's financial reporting goals versus actual performance
original_label: Enron's financial reporting goals versus actual performance
quote: By 1999, Enron was increasingly dependent on transactions with SPEs to close the gap between its actual business performance and its financial reporting goals.
context: Charging document describes Enron management's stated objectives and the pressure created by the gap between what the company reported and what it actually achieved.

label: Manipulate earnings and cash flow to meet quarterly targets
original_label: Manipulate earnings and cash flow to meet quarterly targets
quote: Merrill Lynch's 'purchase' allowed FASTOW, BOYLE, and others to cause Enron to record improperly $12 million in earnings and $28 million in funds flow in the fourth quarter of 1999.
context: Charging document describes how the Nigerian barge transaction was specifically designed to meet quarterly earnings targets.

label: Recognize earnings from troubled project to meet targets
original_label: Recognize earnings from troubled project to meet targets
quote: This purported sale enabled Enron to recognize a total of approximately $65 million of income in the third and fourth quarter of 1999, when it was struggling to meet its projected financial results.
context: Charging document describes the Cuiaba transaction designed specifically to close a gap with projected financial results.

label: Cuiaba project significantly over budget
original_label: Cuiaba project significantly over budget
quote: The Cuiaba project had caused Enron to incur significant costs and by 2001 was approximately over $200 million over budget.
context: Charging document describes an underperforming asset that threatened Enron's financial reporting goals.

label: Failed to find third-party buyer for asset
original_label: Failed to find third-party buyer for asset
quote: When no true third-party buyer could be found, FASTOW and others arranged on September 30, 1999 to 'sell' a portion of Enron's interest in the Cuiaba project to LJM for $11.3 million.
context: Charging document shows that the company could not meet its goals through legitimate market transactions and turned to internal SPE structures.

label: Failed to sell Nigerian barge interest to third parties
original_label: Failed to sell Nigerian barge interest to third parties
quote: In 1999, Enron made unsuccessful efforts to sell an interest in the barges to third parties. When Enron failed to sell the project by December 1999, Enron through FASTOW, BOYLE and others arranged for Merrill Lynch to 'buy' a $28 million interest in the project.
context: Charging document describes how Enron could not liquidate an underperforming asset through normal market channels and turned to artificial transactions.

label: Enron retained hidden interest in RADR despite divestment appearance
original_label: Enron retained hidden interest in RADR despite divestment appearance
quote: In early 1997, FASTOW and others implemented a scheme to reap the proceeds from the farms for themselves, without the farms losing their valuable QF status. As part of the scheme, Enron appeared to divest itself partially of its interest in the farms through a sale to an SPE known as RADR. In reality, Enron retained an illegal and secret interest in the farms; FASTOW and his wife funded the purported independent 3% equity in RADR; and FASTOW and another Enron finance executive, Michael Kopper, controlled distribution of RADR proceeds, which they directed to themselves, friends, and families.
context: Charging document describes the decision to create a fraudulent structure that preserved Enron's benefits while appearing to comply with regulations.

label: Funded SPE's independent equity with concealed loans
original_label: Funded SPE's independent equity with concealed loans
quote: Enron funded 97% of the purchase price with a $16.49 million loan to RADR. Nominees chosen by FASTOW and Kopper contributed the vast majority of the $510,000 that was supposed to constitute the independent 3% equity in RADR. FASTOW and his wife contributed $419,000 of that sum through concealed loans.
context: Charging document describes the decision to create the appearance of independent third-party equity required by accounting rules while actually maintaining control.

label: Farms would lose QF status if Enron became utility holding company
original_label: Farms would lose QF status if Enron became utility holding company
quote: Under applicable federal regulations, wind farms that were more than fifty percent owned by an electric utility holding company were ineligible for QF status, and accordingly were not entitled to the associated financial benefits. By at least late 1996, FASTOW knew that the farms would lose their QF status because Enron was in the process of acquiring Portland General Electric, and as a consequence Enron would become an electric utility holding company.
context: Charging document describes the regulatory constraint that made legitimate continuation of benefits impossible, creating pressure for the RADR scheme.

label: Created Chewco to buy out CALPERS interest while Fastow remained hidden
original_label: Created Chewco to buy out CALPERS interest while Fastow remained hidden
quote: FASTOW proposed the creation of an SPE known as Chewco to buy CALPERS' interest in JEDI. Although FASTOW at first planned to serve as Chewco's outside equity investor and general partner, Kopper was substituted when FASTOW learned that his own involvement would trigger financial disclosure obligations for Enron.
context: Charging document describes the decision to structure a deal to avoid disclosure while maintaining control through Kopper.

label: Authorized improper payments to Chewco for personal benefit
original_label: Authorized improper payments to Chewco for personal benefit
quote: While FASTOW was precluded from serving in an official role at Chewco, he nevertheless demanded and received a portion of Chewco's proceeds from Kopper, in violation of FASTOW's duty to provide honest services to Enron and its shareholders. For example, in December 1998, FASTOW improperly authorized Enron to pay a $400,000 'nuisance/arrangement fee' to Chewco to obtain its consent to amend the JEDI partnership agreement, even though the amendment was for the benefit of Chewco, not Enron.
context: Charging document describes the decision to cause Enron to make payments for personal kickback purposes rather than legitimate business reasons.

label: Board approved Fastow participation in LJM for regular asset off-loading
original_label: Board approved Fastow participation in LJM for regular asset off-loading
quote: By June 1999, in order to have an off-balance-sheet SPE to which Enron regularly could turn, Enron's Board of Directors (the 'Board') agreed to permit FASTOW to create and serve as the managing partner of a new SPE known as LJM Cayman.
context: Charging document describes the establishment of LJM specifically as a structural means to achieve the goal of moving assets off-balance-sheet regularly.

label: LJM transactions designed to manipulate reported financial results
original_label: LJM transactions designed to manipulate reported financial results
quote: From approximately July 1999 through October 2001, Enron entered into transactions with LJM that defrauded Enron, its shareholders, the SEC, credit rating agencies, and others. The transactions with LJM enabled Enron to: (a) manipulate its reported financial results by readily and unobtrusively moving poorly performing assets off balance sheet, when in fact such off-balance-sheet treatment was improper; (b) conceal Enron's poor operating performance by engaging in transactions designed to close gaps between Enron's actual business results and its stated financial reporting goals; (c) manufacture earnings through sham transactions when Enron was having trouble otherwise meeting its goals for a quarter; and (d) improperly inflate the value of Enron's investment portfolio by backdating transaction documents to dates advantageous to Enron.
context: Charging document describes the systematic purpose of LJM transactions as creating false financial appearance to meet reporting goals.

label: Enron and management secretly agreed to prop up LJM
original_label: Enron and management secretly agreed to prop up LJM
quote: In fact, Enron senior management, including FASTOW and GLISAN, secretly agreed that Enron would prop up LJM so that, over time, LJM would not lose money in its dealings with Enron.
context: Charging document describes the decision to enter into hidden arrangements guaranteeing LJM profits contrary to Board representations.

label: Asset parking deals with predetermined repurchase arrangements
original_label: Asset parking deals with predetermined repurchase arrangements
quote: Several transactions between Enron and LJM were mere 'parking' or 'warehousing' deals in which assets were 'sold' to LJM so that Enron could book earnings and record cash flows. FASTOW and others secretly agreed that LJM would hold the asset for a limited time, after which Enron would arrange a repurchase of the assets at a profit to LJM.
context: Charging document describes the decision to structure fake sales as a means to artificially recognize earnings.

label: Promised Merrill Lynch fixed rate and six-month exit to justify barge purchase
original_label: Promised Merrill Lynch fixed rate and six-month exit to justify barge purchase
quote: Enron agreed to finance 75% of the purchase price and only require Merrill Lynch to put up $7 million. Merrill Lynch agreed to 'purchase' the interest only because FASTOW orally promised that Merrill Lynch would receive a fixed interest rate and that Enron would make sure that Merrill Lynch held the barge interest for no more than six months.
context: Charging document describes oral promises designed to induce Merrill Lynch to participate in what was actually a temporary parking transaction.

label: Undisclosed side deal with LJM to guarantee LJM return on Talon
original_label: Undisclosed side deal with LJM to guarantee LJM return on Talon
quote: As FASTOW, GLISAN, and others knew, however, Talon was not properly off balance sheet. First, as FASTOW, GLISAN, and others knew, Enron and FASTOW entered into a secret side agreement whereby Enron guaranteed that it would pay $41 million to LJM before Talon would engage in the hedging transactions for which it was created. In exchange, FASTOW allowed Enron to use Talon to manipulate Enron's financial statements.
context: Charging document describes the decision to create a secret guarantee rendering LJM's investment not at risk despite accounting rule requirements.

label: Manufactured false business purpose to disguise side deal payment
original_label: Manufactured false business purpose to disguise side deal payment
quote: In order to mask the side deal, FASTOW, GLISAN and others devised a scheme to manufacture an ostensible reason for a $41 million payment from Enron to LJM. To do so, Enron and Talon entered into a 'put,' that is, a transaction that purportedly served to hedge Enron against a decline in its own stock value. Although there was no true business purpose, the 'put' option was purchased by Enron for $41 million.
context: Charging document describes the creation of a fake hedge transaction to provide false justification for a payment that was actually the guarantee.

label: Backdated hedge documents to inflate AVICI stock valuation
original_label: Backdated hedge documents to inflate AVICI stock valuation
quote: For example, Enron used a back-dated hedge to fraudulently inflate the value of its investment in 1.09 million shares of AVICI stock. Specifically, FASTOW and others caused documents related to the hedge to be backdated to August 3, 2000, when the price of AVICI reached an all time high of $163.50. In fact, the share price by the actual date of the hedge had declined significantly. By backdating the hedge transaction to August 3, 2000, Enron was able to falsely record the value of its AVICI shares at a significantly inflated price.
context: Charging document describes the decision to falsify transaction dates to capture higher valuations and manipulate financial statements.

label: Fastow and Kopper fraudulently induced NatWest to sell at false price
original_label: Fastow and Kopper fraudulently induced NatWest to sell at false price
quote: It was part of the scheme that FASTOW, Kopper, and the NatWest bankers fraudulently induced NatWest to sell its interest in Swap Sub for $1 million, at a time when they knew the interest was worth millions more. Indeed, on or about March 22, 2000, FASTOW finalized an agreement with Enron to pay Swap Sub $30 million to unwind Enron's transactions with Swap Sub. FASTOW represented to Enron that CSFB would receive $10 million, and falsely represented that NatWest would receive $20 million. In fact, as FASTOW, GLISAN, and others knew, NatWest received only $1 million.
context: Charging document describes the decision to misrepresent the value of NatWest's interest to induce them to sell at a steep loss.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Fastow received over $100,000 from RADR proceeds
original_label: Fastow received over $100,000 from RADR proceeds
quote: Between approximately December 1997 and February 2000, FASTOW and his family received over $100,000 in additional RADR proceeds.
context: Charging document describes personal financial benefit that Fastow realized from manipulating the RADR transaction structure.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Fastow received $67,224 in kickbacks from Chewco payment
original_label: Fastow received $67,224 in kickbacks from Chewco payment
quote: In December 1998 and January 1999, FASTOW received kickbacks from that payment totaling $67,224, in the form of checks from Kopper to FASTOW and FASTOW's family.
context: Charging document describes personal compensation received by Fastow tied to authorizing improper Enron payments.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Southampton fraud scheme distributed $19 million to conspirators
original_label: Southampton fraud scheme distributed $19 million to conspirators
quote: The $19 million of illegal proceeds was divided among the conspirators. The NatWest bankers received approximately $7.3 million. The remaining balance of the funds went to 'investors' in a partnership known as Southampton. These 'investors,' their 'investments,' and their returns were as follows: FASTOW Family Foundation $25,000 $4,465,000; Michael Kopper $25,000 $4,465,000; BEN F. GLISAN, JR. $5,826 $1,040,744; Other Enron/LJM Employees $13,339 $2,392,000.
context: Charging document describes the distribution of massive returns from the Southampton scheme to Fastow, Glisan and others tied to their fraud participation.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Fastow sold $18.1 million in Enron stock while committing fraud
original_label: Fastow sold $18.1 million in Enron stock while committing fraud
quote: During the period relevant to this Indictment, FASTOW sold approximately 235,117 shares of Enron stock, generating gross proceeds of $18,143,443.50.
context: Charging document describes substantial personal gains from selling Enron stock while engaging in the fraud schemes.

label: Fastow violated board representation against personal stock profit
original_label: Fastow violated board representation against personal stock profit
quote: FASTOW violated his representation to the Board that he would not personally profit from any appreciation in the value of Enron shares held by LJM.
context: Charging document describes Fastow's decision to violate explicit board assurances made to secure approval for LJM participation.

label: False representations to Board about transaction review and disclosure
original_label: False representations to Board about transaction review and disclosure
quote: FASTOW and others made various false representations to Enron's Board to obtain its approval for FASTOW's participation in LJM. Specifically, the Board was assured that: (a) Enron's Chief Accounting and Chief Risk Officers would review all transactions with LJM to ensure their fairness to Enron; (b) the Board would be informed of all Enron transactions with LJM; (c) the purpose of LJM was to buy assets from Enron and enable Enron to hedge certain investments; and (d) although FASTOW would be compensated by LJM, he would not have a pecuniary interest in the Enron stock held by LJM or its affiliates.
context: Charging document describes deliberate misrepresentations made to secure board approval for LJM.

label: Board not informed of LJM asset repurchases at profit
original_label: Board not informed of LJM asset repurchases at profit
quote: As FASTOW and others further knew, although the Board was told that LJM was a vehicle to which Enron could sell assets, and that it would be informed of all transactions with LJM, the Board was not informed that Enron would from time to time repurchase assets from LJM, or find another buyer, at a profit to LJM. Indeed, in presentations to the Board about Enron's transactions with LJM, Enron's senior management failed to report on transactions in which Enron repurchased assets from LJM.
context: Charging document describes deliberate withholding of material information from the Board about how LJM transactions actually worked.

label: Rhythms Net shares locked up, unable to sell through market
original_label: Rhythms Net shares locked up, unable to sell through market
quote: Enron was at risk for market price fluctuations in Rhythms Net shares. Because Enron was restricted from selling its shares until November 1999, it sought to reduce the impact on its financial results of a possible dramatic decline in the share price of Rhythms Net stock.
context: Charging document describes the legitimate constraint that motivated the creation of the fraudulent Swap Sub hedge.

label: Enron unable to find sixth-month buyer for Merrill Lynch barge interest
original_label: Enron unable to find sixth-month buyer for Merrill Lynch barge interest
quote: With no true third-party purchaser available to buy Merrill Lynch's interest as the six-month deadline loomed, on June 29, 2000, FASTOW, GLISAN, BOYLE, and others arranged for LJM to purchase Merrill Lynch's interest.
context: Charging document describes the failure to find a legitimate third-party buyer, forcing reliance on the internal LJM structure.

label: IPO lock-up agreements prevented normal stock sales
original_label: IPO lock-up agreements prevented normal stock sales
quote: Following an IPO, Enron was at risk for market price fluctuations in the shares, many of which were extremely volatile. Because Enron was restricted by 'lock up' agreements from selling these shares until some future date, it sought to reduce the impact on its financial results of a possible dramatic decline in the share price.
context: Charging document describes the regulatory constraint that prevented Enron from managing its stock portfolio through normal market sales.

label: Enron struggling to meet projected financial results in Q3 and Q4 1999
original_label: Enron struggling to meet projected financial results in Q3 and Q4 1999
quote: This purported sale enabled Enron to recognize a total of approximately $65 million of income in the third and fourth quarter of 1999, when it was struggling to meet its projected financial results.
context: Charging document describes the specific timing of the Cuiaba transaction linked to quarterly earnings shortfall.

label: LJM would meet prearranged rate of return through Enron support
original_label: LJM would meet prearranged rate of return through Enron support
quote: LJM would meet its pre-arranged rate of return, as Enron senior management secretly agreed that LJM losses would be made up by Enron in other deals.
context: Charging document describes the target return for LJM that was guaranteed regardless of actual transaction performance.

label: Made false and misleading public statements about financial performance
original_label: Made false and misleading public statements about financial performance
quote: Enron's making false and misleading public statements about Enron's financial performance.
context: Charging document lists false public statements as one of the means used to execute the schemes.

label: Filed materially false and misleading financial statements with SEC
original_label: Filed materially false and misleading financial statements with SEC
quote: Enron's filing materially false and misleading financial statements with the SEC.
context: Charging document lists filing false statements with SEC as one of the means used to execute the schemes.

label: Took advantage of Fastow's simultaneous control over SPEs and operations
original_label: Took advantage of Fastow's simultaneous control over SPEs and operations
quote: FASTOW's and others' taking advantage of FASTOW's simultaneous control over SPEs and Enron's business operations.
context: Charging document describes the structural choice to exploit Fastow's dual role for personal benefit.

label: Made false representations to outside auditors about Merrill Lynch agreement
original_label: Made false representations to outside auditors about Merrill Lynch agreement
quote: In or about December 1999, Enron made false representations to its outside auditors regarding the terms of the agreement between Merrill Lynch and Enron.
context: Charging document describes the decision to misrepresent transaction terms to auditors in the Nigerian barge scheme.

label: Made false representations to auditors about LJM-Merrill Lynch agreement
original_label: Made false representations to auditors about LJM-Merrill Lynch agreement
quote: In or about June 2000, Enron made false representations to its outside auditors regarding the agreement between Merrill Lynch, Enron and LJM.
context: Charging document describes subsequent misrepresentations to auditors about the revised transaction structure.

label: Approved payment against advice of inside and outside counsel
original_label: Approved payment against advice of inside and outside counsel
quote: Against the advice of both inside and outside counsel at Enron, FASTOW approved the payment to Chewco.
context: Charging document describes Fastow's decision to override legal advice to authorize an improper payment.

label: Disguised income as gifts to avoid tax reporting
original_label: Disguised income as gifts to avoid tax reporting
quote: So that his concealed interest in RADR would not be revealed, at FASTOW's direction the payments were mischaracterized as 'gifts' from Kopper and a nominee to FASTOW, his wife, and two children. FASTOW and his wife did not report to their accountants or in their federal income tax returns to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) any of the RADR income disguised as gifts.
context: Charging document describes the decision to hide income by labeling it as gifts to avoid tax reporting requirements.

label: Did not report kickback income on tax returns
original_label: Did not report kickback income on tax returns
quote: FASTOW and his wife did not report those kickbacks to their tax accountants or as income on their 1998 and 1999 federal income tax returns to the IRS.
context: Charging document describes Fastow's failure to report kickback income on federal tax returns.

label: Delayed Cuiaba asset repurchase sale until after Fastow divested LJM
original_label: Delayed Cuiaba asset repurchase sale until after Fastow divested LJM
quote: In order to avoid public disclosure of Enron's repurchase of LJM's Cuiaba interest at an unwarranted profit, the sale was deliberately delayed by FASTOW and others until after FASTOW had divested his interest in LJM.
context: Charging document describes the deliberate timing of disclosure to avoid revealing Fastow's personal stake.

label: Enron's SPEs designed to improve reported financial results
original_label: Enron's SPEs designed to improve reported financial results
quote: Since the 1990's, Enron engaged in transactions with SPEs that were designed to improve Enron's reported financial results.
context: Charging document describes the stated purpose of SPE transactions as improving reported financial results.

label: Off-balance-sheet accounting to present company more attractively to analysts
original_label: Off-balance-sheet accounting to present company more attractively to analysts
quote: Enron's management, including FASTOW and GLISAN, and others, including BOYLE, preferred the latter result, known as 'off-balance-sheet,' because it enabled Enron to (a) book earnings and record cash flow and (b) avoid inclusion of unfavorable information in its reported financial statements, thereby presenting itself more attractively to Wall Street investment analysts, credit rating agencies, the investing public, and others.
context: Charging document describes management's explicit preference for off-balance-sheet structures to influence perceptions.

label: Conspired to defraud investors about Enron financial results
original_label: Conspired to defraud investors about Enron financial results
quote: Between at least 1996 and November 2001, FASTOW, GLISAN, BOYLE and others devised various schemes to defraud Enron and its shareholders, the investing public, the SEC, and others. The goals of the schemes included: (a) fraudulent manipulation of Enron's reported financial results so that Enron would appear more successful than it was; (b) artificial manipulation of the share price of Enron stock; (c) circumvention of federal regulations so that Enron could obtain benefits to which it was not entitled.
context: Charging document describes the overall conspiracy to defraud investors through manipulation of reported results.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Personal enrichment at expense of honest services duty
original_label: Personal enrichment at expense of honest services duty
quote: personal enrichment of FASTOW, GLISAN, BOYLE, and others at the expense of Enron, its shareholders, and others to whom they owed a duty of honest services.
context: Charging document identifies personal financial benefit as one of the core goals of the fraud schemes.

label: Analyst expectations and stock price targets
original_label: Analyst expectations and stock price targets
quote: The problem I have with it is it keeps the stock price inflated. And you had Mr. Skilling saying our stock price was going to go to $120 per share.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies about the growth ambitions and public targets communicated by Skilling to the market.

label: Earnings targets and meeting street expectations
original_label: Earnings targets and meeting street expectations
quote: It was very common knowledge. It wasn't hidden. There were people like Mr. McMahon and others that had expressed concerns about LJM and the transactions Enron was doing with LJM. But for the most part, people seemed to think there was some accounting rule that was allowing this to be acceptable.
context: Ms. Watkins describes how colleagues understood the Raptor transactions as a means to meet financial targets, treated as common knowledge across the organization.

label: Projected earnings per share and market multiples
original_label: Projected earnings per share and market multiples
quote: It was important that we announce that Enron Energy Services was profitable in 2000. Without the New Power hedges, EES was not profitable in 2000. This would have significantly impacted our PE multiples and our stock price in the year 2000.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies about the explicit connection between hitting profitability targets and maintaining the company's valuation multiple.

label: Cannot hedge at market rates with real third parties
original_label: Cannot hedge at market rates with real third parties
quote: I doubt we could have hedged these volatile stocks with any true unrelated third party at the prices that we were actually able to obtain from Raptor. It is my opinion that he was probably aware that we could not have transacted at those prices with an unrelated third party, and the only reason Mr. Fastow was transacting with Enron through the Raptor transactions at those prices for volatile stocks was that Mr. Fastow could not lose money and he was backstopped by Enron stock.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the terms available from legitimate third-party hedgers were prohibitively expensive compared to the Raptor structures, revealing why the deviant path was taken.

label: No legitimate third party would accept hedge terms
original_label: No legitimate third party would accept hedge terms
quote: Well, I don't think you could have locked it in at that $170 price. There would have been a significant haircut to that price. As much as, I would say, 30 or 40 percent. Probably more like $120 or $110, maybe even lower.
context: Mr. Deutsch and Ms. Watkins discuss the cost of legitimate hedges, establishing why real alternatives were foreclosed by expense.

label: Analyst scrutiny of cash flow versus earnings mismatch
original_label: Analyst scrutiny of cash flow versus earnings mismatch
quote: Wall Street analysts began to distrust Enron's increasingly complex earnings statements, so they started examining the company's cashflow. After all, cash is cash. However, since Enron had been manipulating its earnings, its cashflow would appear inadequate compared to its inflated earnings statements. This was a problem for Enron, was it not?
context: Mr. Strickland and Ms. Watkins discuss the capital markets' skepticism driving Enron to inflate cash-from-operations metrics.

label: Capital markets demand high valuation multiple
original_label: Capital markets demand high valuation multiple
quote: Enron did not want to be characterized as a normal trading company. The analysts were concerned that our funds flow from operations was significantly lower than our earnings. It was a financial performance statistic that they were concerned about, and Enron attempted to fix that first, fairly legitimately, by securitizing contracts and selling them out to outside third parties.
context: Ms. Watkins explains how trading company multiples (12-14x) fell short of Enron's ambitions, creating pressure to manipulate cash-flow metrics.

label: Fastow uses strongarm tactics with banks to invest in LJM
original_label: Fastow uses strongarm tactics with banks to invest in LJM
quote: I had heard from friends that worked at Chase and Credit Suisse and Bank of America that Mr. Fastow was almost somewhat threatening, that if you didn't invest in LJM, Enron would not use you as a banker or an investment banker again. That he was threatening the institutions, that to get Enron business they should invest in LJM.
context: Ms. Watkins describes how external pressure from dependent financial institutions was leveraged to fund the LJM partnerships.

label: Raptor vehicles underwater and required constant cash injection
original_label: Raptor vehicles underwater and required constant cash injection
quote: Raptor owed Enron in excess of $700 million, and there was not an outside third party that bore that loss. It was going to be borne by Enron's shareholders by an issuance of stock in the future. My main point to Mr. Lay was that by this time Raptor owed Enron in excess of $700 million under certain hedging agreements. My understanding was that the Raptor entities basically had no other business aside from these hedges. Therefore, they had collectively lost over $700 million.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies about the mounting losses in the Raptor vehicles that required constant capital infusions to prevent collapse.

label: Hedged assets declining in value faster than projected
original_label: Hedged assets declining in value faster than projected
quote: The investments that were probably the more volatile was the tech investment in Avici and the New Power Company, a startup that Enron had done. Those investments were hedged with Raptor. They had dropped significantly in value, and in the related party footnote in 2000 it mentions that Enron had recognized $500 million of revenue from the special entities' offsetting of corresponding writedown in the equity investment portfolio of Enron.
context: Ms. Watkins describes the deteriorating value of core merchant investments that the Raptor structures were designed to conceal.

label: EBS and EES massive losses hidden by Raptor hedges
original_label: EBS and EES massive losses hidden by Raptor hedges
quote: The Raptor hedge on Avici made EBS look like it had only lost $50 or $60 million in 2000 when actually it was more like $250 million. And it was very important to Enron that we announce that Enron Energy Services was profitable in 2000. Without the New Power hedges, EES was not profitable in 2000.
context: Ms. Watkins explains how Raptor structures concealed massive operating losses in the growth divisions.

label: Chief Risk Officer feared disaster if earnings targets missed
original_label: Chief Risk Officer feared disaster if earnings targets missed
quote: Mr. Buy expressed the opinion to me, as early as maybe even 1997/1998, that he felt like Enron was one or two quarters away from disaster. Now, he had different reasons for that, but that was because we were a trading company. Trading companies usually it is hard to predict earnings. You have to depend upon volatility in the marketplace. And we were so dead set on predicting our earnings, and the street had become accustomed to us predicting our earnings. So he just felt like if we ever missed our earnings targets people, i.e. the analysts and the investing community, would look at us under a microscope and that he was concerned that would put us in in a disastrous position.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies about the CRO's early recognition that missing earnings would trigger catastrophic market repricing.

label: Stock price decline triggers credit rating threat
original_label: Stock price decline triggers credit rating threat
quote: When the investing community was uncertain about our numbers, when they were driving the stock price down, almost everyone was aware that if the stock price dropped too low, if our investment grade rating fell away, there would be additional debt coming due. And we did have an old-fashioned run on the bank.
context: Ms. Watkins explains the feedback loop between equity market skepticism, stock price decline, and credit rating downgrades.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Performance ranking based on last six months only
original_label: Performance ranking based on last six months only
quote: Everyone was very conscious of what they were contributing in the last 6 months. The performance ranking system judged you on what you contributed to the company in the last 6 months. No old tapes. In that sense, it was very competitive.
context: Mr. Rush and Ms. Watkins discuss Enron's high-powered incentive scheme that encouraged short-term focus.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Insiders sold billions while stock was inflated by Raptor gains
original_label: Insiders sold billions while stock was inflated by Raptor gains
quote: you know, these people were wise enough or lucky enough to sell stocks before the facts that you have described and that we have uncovered became public. And it is either they were all very lucky or, in fact, they were trading on inside information, as it appears from the outside looking in. Total of 17 million shares. You know, obviously, none of these shares were sold at zero, at a dollar, at $5, at $10.
context: Mr. Deutsch notes that Enron insiders systematically sold shares at peak prices maintained by Raptor accounting gains.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: LJM investors earned 2503% annual returns on eight-day investments
original_label: LJM investors earned 2503% annual returns on eight-day investments
quote: As described in an LJM2 presentation to its partners in October of 2000, Raptor III, for example, paid out $41 million on a $30 million investment in just 8 days. This is an amazing 2,503 percent annual return for those investors.
context: Mr. Dingell notes the extraordinary returns available to insiders through LJM2 partnerships structured around Raptor vehicles.

label: Mandate to sell merchant assets into special purpose entities
original_label: Mandate to sell merchant assets into special purpose entities
quote: Enron's risk and finance departments had put out the word that all divisions should sell merchant assets to White Wing by the end of the third and fourth quarters of 1999. Besides that mandate, was there any other reason for Enron to sell Promigas to White Wing at that time?
context: Mr. Strickland and Ms. Watkins describe how senior leadership issued binding directives to business units to meet cash-flow targets.

label: Targets for funds flow from operations imposed on business units
original_label: Targets for funds flow from operations imposed on business units

label: American Airlines threatens to order Airbus instead
original_label: American Airlines threatens to order Airbus instead

context: Report describes how competitive pressure from Airbus's A320neo forced Boeing to reverse its strategy and re-engine the 737 rather than develop a clean-sheet aircraft.

label: Design objective to achieve Level B pilot training
original_label: Design objective to achieve Level B pilot training
quote: One of the principal goals of the 737 MAX program was that it would require no greater than Level B differences training for pilots to transition from flying the 737 NG to flying the 737 MAX aircraft. Even before an AR approved of the Boeing employee plan to describe MCAS as merely an addition to the speed trim system, efforts to avoid increased pilot training requirements were already well underway throughout the 737 MAX program. On Saturday, May 4, 2013, several weeks before the MCAS strategy meeting referenced above, Michael Teal, the former Chief Project Engineer on the 737 MAX program, sent an email to senior chiefs and functional leaders on the MAX program and listed 14 open significant trade studies/risk issues. One of them specifically addressed the concern that MCAS could increase pilot training requirements: Differences Pilot Training: Ensuring that the level of change on the MAX keeps the Differences training to 16 hours or less of Level B training. In a transcribed interview with Committee staff, Mr. Teal acknowledged that obtaining Level B training on the 737 MAX was a design objective of the MAX program and that he had a role in ensuring that design objective was being met.
context: Report documents that the Chief Project Engineer explicitly stated that achieving Level B training was a design objective set for the MAX program, constraining other technical choices.

label: Cost of re-engining versus building new aircraft
original_label: Cost of re-engining versus building new aircraft
quote: In 2011, the estimated cost of building a brand-new airplane hovered around $10 billion while the cost of re-engining the existing 737 NG to develop the new 737 MAX airplane was only about $3 billion, according to Richard Aboulafia with the aviation industry market analysis firm, the Teal Group. Multiple current and former Boeing employees who have contacted the Committee since our investigation began have relayed dismay at the path they believe Boeing has taken since its merger with McDonnell Douglas. They have described their excitement and enthusiasm at joining one of the world's most esteemed companies decades ago. They were thrilled to be working with smart, intelligent, and dedicated colleagues. They viewed Boeing as an engineer's paradise where they could innovate and create leading edge technologies where safety was always at the forefront of engineering decisions that were part and parcel of the business development process. However, that emphasis changed slowly, but dramatically, over the years, according to these employees. The prowess of the engineers' technical designs and innovative diagrams were replaced by the accounting acumen and financial decisions of business executives. Production schedules and monetary costs, not technical specifications and safety considerations, began to drive Boeing's commercial aircraft programs, they say.
context: Report explains that Boeing chose to re-engine the 737 rather than develop a new aircraft because of cost constraints ($3 billion versus $10 billion), and describes how financial pressures began to dominate over engineering and safety considerations.

label: Schedule pressure and countdown clock
original_label: Schedule pressure and countdown clock
quote: To emphasize the significance of the 737 MAX program's schedule to Boeing employees, the Committee learned that senior program officials kept a countdown clock in their conference room. Keith Leverkuhn, the former Vice President and General Manager of the MAX program, described the clock as an excitement generator for Boeing's staff. But he also acknowledged it was to remind staff about the MAX's schedule. One of the mantras that we had was the value of a day, he said, and making sure that we were being prudent with our time, that we were being thorough, but yet, that there was a schedule that needed to be met. He said the countdown clock was used to mark two major milestones: power on, when the MAX was powered up for the first time in the factory, and first flight.
context: Report describes how Boeing's senior leadership communicated schedule as an overriding imperative through a visible countdown clock, framing each day as precious.

label: Cost reductions in avionics testing and simulator hours
original_label: Cost reductions in avionics testing and simulator hours

context: Report documents explicit cost-cutting decisions that reduced safety-critical testing on the 737 MAX program.

label: Synthetic airspeed rejected due to training and cost concerns
original_label: Synthetic airspeed rejected due to training and cost concerns

However, this request was rejected by Boeing management due to cost concerns and because adding synthetic airspeed could have jeopardized the 737 MAX program's directive to avoid pilot simulator training requirements.
context: Report shows that a safety enhancement (synthetic airspeed) was explicitly rejected because it conflicted with the design objective of achieving Level B training and cost targets.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets

original_label: Chief Project Engineer rewarded with stock for meeting schedule

label: Senior program manager dismisses safety concerns over profit
original_label: Senior program manager dismisses safety concerns over profit

Mr. Pierson described multiple concerns about production and schedule pressures that were impacting quality control and safety issues. As a retired Naval Officer and former Squadron Commanding Officer, wrote Pierson, I know how dangerous even the smallest of defects can be to the safety of an airplane. Frankly right now all my internal warning bells are going off. And for the first time in my life, I'm sorry to say that I'm hesitant about putting my family on a Boeing airplane. In July 2018, five weeks after Mr. Pierson's email, he finally met with Mr. Campbell in Mr. Campbell's office. According to Mr. Pierson's testimony to the Committee, he told Mr. Campbell that in the military they would temporarily halt production if they had the kinds of safety problems that Mr. Pierson was seeing on the MAX factory floor. Mr. Campbell allegedly responded: The military is not a profit-making organization.
context: Report documents how a safety-conscious plant supervisor raised urgent concerns to a senior manager, who responded by dismissing them in favor of profit considerations, illustrating pressure transmission.

label: Effort to downplay MCAS as speed trim addition to avoid training impact
original_label: Effort to downplay MCAS as speed trim addition to avoid training impact
quote: In May 2013, a group of Boeing employees working on the 737 MAX met to address another concern: If we emphasize MCAS is a new function there may be greater certification and training impact, one Boeing employee wrote in a June 7, 2013, email summarizing the minutes of that meeting. While Boeing did not hide MCAS from regulators, or even some airlines, it appears Boeing took efforts over the lifespan of the MAX program to downplay and deflect attention away from MCAS even after the Lion Air crash. The Boeing employees that devised the MCAS strategy were not the only Boeing employees that appeared to worry about the consequences that MCAS could cause to the 737 MAX's certification and pilot training requirements. The intent of this plan was clear. It was not to avoid confusion about MCAS by regulators or 737 MAX pilots. The purpose of characterizing MCAS as an addition to speed trim was to avoid greater certification and training impact. Boeing's item tracking compliance system database, called ITRACS, that documented this decision suggested that cost was also a factor in the plan to downplay MCAS and to describe it as merely an addition to the Speed Trim System. On May 21, 2013, as part of that strategy meeting, the issue was presented this way in Boeing's ITRACS database: Problem Statement: Every new buzzword represents a company and airline cost via changed manuals, changed training, changed maintenance manuals. Recommended Action: Investigate deletion of MCAS nomenclature and cover under the umbrella of revised speed trim.
context: Report documents Boeing employees' explicit strategy to describe MCAS as an addition to speed trim rather than as a new system, motivated by avoiding costs and training/certification impacts.

label: Plan to treat MCAS externally as speed trim addition
original_label: Plan to treat MCAS externally as speed trim addition

The Boeing employees also agreed to make sure that their technical familiarity presentation to the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) is consistent with the intent that MCAS is an addition to Speed Trim. The Boeing AR concurred with Boeing's plan regarding its description of MCAS. As stated in the summary of the meeting, This will allow us to maintain the MCAS nomenclature while not driving additional work due to training impacts and maintenance manual expansions.
context: Report documents that Boeing sought approval from its Authorized Representative for a plan to characterize MCAS externally as speed trim addition to avoid training and maintenance impacts.

label: Southwest Airlines discount clause creates financial constraint on training
original_label: Southwest Airlines discount clause creates financial constraint on training

Under a contract signed in December 2011 with Southwest Airlines, the U.S. launch customer for the 737 MAX, Boeing was financially obligated to have discounted the price of each MAX airplane it delivered to Southwest by at least $1 million if the FAA had required simulator training for pilots transitioning from the 737 NG to the 737 MAX. Southwest had 200 firm orders for the MAX with the option to purchase an additional 191 MAX aircraft. Thus, if Boeing failed to obtain Level B (non-simulator) training requirements or less from the FAA it would have owed Southwest between $200 to nearly $400 million. This helped incentivize Boeing and its leadership to forestall any simulator training for 737 MAX pilots. This had the impact of evading and averting the inclusion of at least one technology that could have affected Boeing's directive to avoid simulator training.
context: Report documents a contractual financial penalty structure that created powerful financial motivation for Boeing to achieve Level B training and avoid simulator requirements.

label: Boeing lost market share to Airbus A320neo
original_label: Boeing lost market share to Airbus A320neo

This translated into significant cost savings for airlines and potentially passengers, and created a competitive advantage for Airbus. But Boeing initially downplayed this competitive threat. At a Boeing Commercial Airplanes (BCA) employee meeting on January 14, 2011, James Albaugh, BCA's CEO, said: I think Airbus will find re-engining the A320 more challenging than they think it will be. He did not think the new Airbus could compete with Boeing's 737 NG aircraft. At the same time, while we haven't made a firm decision, I don't think we will re-engine the 737.

label: Need to match Airbus A320neo to retain market share
original_label: Need to match Airbus A320neo to retain market share
quote: But a call to Albaugh's boss changed that position. The call was reportedly serious and the conversation frank. Boeing was told that American Airlines was about to close a deal to purchase hundreds of A320-family airplanes from Airbus. context: Report explains how the threat of losing American Airlines as a customer to Airbus forced Boeing's hand and led to the strategic reversal to re-engine the 737 instead of developing a new aircraft.

label: Boeing announced intent to re-engine 737 despite prior skepticism
original_label: Boeing announced intent to re-engine 737 despite prior skepticism

label: MCAS reliance on single AOA sensor questioned but not changed
original_label: MCAS reliance on single AOA sensor questioned but not changed

label: EICAS exception to avoid costs and training impacts
original_label: EICAS exception to avoid costs and training impacts
quote: Boeing obtained an FAA exception to allow the company to not install an Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System (EICAS) on the 737 MAX. Since 1982, an EICAS or its equivalent among Airbus airplanes has been common in newly certificated transport aircraft. It displays aircraft system faults and failures in the cockpit and helps pilots prioritize responding to multiple or simultaneous indications and alerts, which are often accompanied by aural alerts specific to the level of severity of a particular fault. But the exception from FAA relieved Boeing of the requirement that the 737 MAX must be equipped with a caution, alert, and advisory system. Boeing was well aware early on of the risk posed to the 737 MAX program if it was required to implement an EICAS on the MAX. In June 2012, a Boeing employee gave a presentation titled: 737 MAX Certification Basis Risk Review: EICAS. The presentation defined the issue this way: Numerous crew alerts on the 737Max are new or revised and per changed product regulation are required to meet latest amendment level. Current 737 flight crew alerting methods won't comply with latest regulation. The presentation went on to say that a compliant design would be similar to the 787 or 767 tanker and include EICAS as well as other features. Significantly, the presentation noted: IF we had to comply outright with regulation: Considerable program cost and schedule risk, it asserted, and significant impact on pilot training requirements.
context: Report documents that Boeing explicitly chose not to install EICAS because compliance would impose considerable program cost, schedule risk, and pilot training impacts.

label: Boeing sought exception from EICAS based on cost and impracticality argument
original_label: Boeing sought exception from EICAS based on cost and impracticality argument

Boeing's exception proposal will be based on compliance with the regulation being impractical. The cost of complying not commensurate with degree of safety improvement, the presentation suggested. The presentation also cited elements of the cost story and said: Also depends on convincing the FAA that the safety improvement of complying with the new rule is not overwhelming. The presentation said the MAX program would need help from Boeing finance personnel regarding how to structure our cost story, and it said that they needed buy-in to such an exception proposal from Boeing's Authorized Representatives (ARs), who are supposed to represent the interests of the FAA. In the end, the FAA accepted Boeing's argument about the impracticality and the economic expense of installing EICAS on the 737 MAX.
context: Report documents Boeing's deliberate strategy to craft a cost-based argument for an exception from EICAS, with specific steps to structure the cost narrative and secure AR buy-in.

label: MCAS redesign in March 2016 increased authority to lower speeds
original_label: MCAS redesign in March 2016 increased authority to lower speeds

label: Boeing removed MCAS references from pilot training after March 2016 redesign
original_label: Boeing removed MCAS references from pilot training after March 2016 redesign

As a result, 737 MAX pilots were precluded from knowing of the existence of MCAS and its potential effect on aircraft handling without pilot command. Meanwhile, the FAA officials who authorized this request remained unaware of the redesign of MCAS until after the crash of the Lion Air flight.
context: Report documents that hours after MCAS was redesigned to have greater authority, Boeing removed references to it from pilot training, and FAA approvers were unaware of the redesign.

label: Boeing marketed Level B training in July 2014 before FAA decision
original_label: Boeing marketed Level B training in July 2014 before FAA decision

original_label: Chief Technical Pilot claimed savings from avoiding simulator training

original_label: Chief Technical Pilot opposed simulator training after Lion Air crash

original_label: Boeing financial losses on 787 Dreamliner production

label: Larger engines on 737 MAX altered aerodynamics requiring MCAS
original_label: Larger engines on 737 MAX altered aerodynamics requiring MCAS
quote: To help accomplish this, Boeing installed, larger, more fuel efficient engines on this new 737 derivative airplane model dubbed the 737 MAX aircraft. The existing engines on the 737 NG aircraft were located under the wings and already hung relatively low to the ground, a vestige of the 737's original 1967 design—a time when stairs were more commonly used by passengers to board planes than jetways, and ground crews more commonly hand-lifted luggage into cargo holds, as opposed to using motorized belt loaders. As a result, there was not enough ground clearance to simply swap out the old engines and replace them with new, larger, more efficient ones. The engines on the 737 NG have a ground clearance of 17 inches. By comparison, Boeing's 757 model aircraft has a minimum clearance of 29 inches and Boeing's 787 Dreamliner has a minimum clearance of 28 inches. The 737 NG engine hangs so low that the otherwise circular casing around it, known as a nacelle, is flattened at the bottom – giving it a look that some pilots have dubbed the hamster pouch.
context: Report explains the technical constraints that resulted from mounting larger engines on the 737, which required software fixes like MCAS.

label: Boeing did not reevaluate MCAS after March 2016 redesign
original_label: Boeing did not reevaluate MCAS after March 2016 redesign

label: Boeing dismissed concerns about MCAS repetitive activation as non-safety issue
original_label: Boeing dismissed concerns about MCAS repetitive activation as non-safety issue

label: Boeing did not share test pilot catastrophic response time data with FAA
original_label: Boeing did not share test pilot catastrophic response time data with FAA

original_label: MCAS vulnerability to single AOA sensor questioned in December 2015

original_label: Boeing stock buybacks and dividends during MAX development

original_label: Boeing AR concerned but colleagues dismissed repetitive MCAS activation risk

original_label: American Airlines commitment secured 100 737 MAX orders

original_label: Southwest Airlines penalty for exceeding training

original_label: Competing with Airbus A320neo

original_label: Aggressive production rate targets

label: Countdown clocks emphasizing schedule
original_label: Countdown clocks emphasizing schedule

The second was 'first flight,' which occurred on January 30, 2016, as scores of Boeing employees watched and applauded as the 737 MAX took off for the first time. The 'countdown clocks' were located in the conference room where the 737 MAX program's senior-most management held 'business performance reviews,' 'technical review boards,' and other meetings. Mr. Leverkuhn acknowledged that it was his 'desire' to install these 'countdown clocks.' He suggested that the countdown clocks were 'an excitement generator to remind people that we were doing something remarkable on the development of the [737 MAX] program.' context: Committee staff interview with Boeing VP/GM on how countdown clocks communicated schedule pressure to employees.

label: Value of a day mantra
original_label: Value of a day mantra

context: Keith Leverkuhn explaining how schedule pressure was communicated as a fundamental mantra.

label: Synthetic airspeed rejected for cost and training impact
original_label: Synthetic airspeed rejected for cost and training impact
quote: Early in the 737 MAX design and development process, Boeing rejected at least one design proposal by Boeing engineers—equipage of a synthetic airspeed indicator on the 737 MAX--due to alleged cost concerns. In 2013, a Boeing employee suggested that it would be a challenge to install a synthetic airspeed indicator on the 737 MAX. However, synthetic airspeed indication was already a basic feature on Boeing's 787 Dreamliner. A Boeing Technical Pilot responded: 'As I pointed out in the telecom today, an introduction of synthetic airspeed to the MAX would drastically alter [the Airspeed Unreliable] Critical Action, Memory Item Non-Normal Checklist. If synthetic airspeed is standard as opposed to an option, it would likely jeopardize the Program directive to maintain Level B training for our customers.'
context: Committee findings on Boeing's rejection of a safety feature due to training requirement implications and cost concerns.

label: Management vetoed synthetic airspeed system
original_label: Management vetoed synthetic airspeed system
quote: However, because the system relies on AOA data as one datapoint, the system can also be used to assess the reliability of AOA sensors. In other words, if AOA data is lost but not announced to the pilots because of the absence of an AOA Disagree alert, the pilots could infer from the simultaneous loss of a synthetic airspeed computation that one or both of the AOA sensors had failed. Therefore, it is possible that inclusion of a synthetic airspeed system on the 737 MAX could have provided the Lion Air flight 610 flight crew with another clue to help them deduce that at least one AOA sensor had failed (the pilots of Ethiopian Airlines flight 302 correctly diagnosed the problem). Unfortunately, the request to install synthetic airspeed on the 737 MAX was rejected by Boeing management because its introduction would have been too costly and may have resulted in the FAA requiring simulator training on the MAX – something that would have jeopardized the 737 MAX program's clear and consistent goal to avoid simulator training requirements.
context: Committee investigation explaining the cost and training rationale for rejecting synthetic airspeed.

label: Manager stated people must die before Boeing changes
original_label: Manager stated people must die before Boeing changes
quote: The notion of adding synthetic airspeed to the MAX was raised three separate times with Boeing managers and rejected on the basis of cost and potential pilot training impacts, according to an internal Boeing complaint filed by a Boeing engineer and reported on by both the Seattle Times and the New York Times. According to the Seattle Times story, Michael Teal cited those reasons when he ultimately made a decision not to include synthetic airspeed on the MAX. According to the Seattle Times, the Boeing employee who filed the complaint said management was more concerned with cost and schedule than safety or quality. The complaint also alleged that Boeing hid inflight safety incident data from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), according to the newspaper. Further, it reported that the employee who filed the complaint expressed concerns about retaliation for even raising these issues internally at Boeing. The Boeing employee apparently wrote, that given 'the nature of this complaint, the fear of retaliation is high, despite all official assurances that this should not be the case. There is a suppressive cultural attitude towards criticism of corporate policy – especially if that criticism comes as a result of fatal accidents.' Even more chilling was that the Boeing engineer who wrote to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation said that in 2015 his Boeing manager argued against including synthetic airspeed on the MAX, reportedly stating, 'People have to die before Boeing will change things.'
context: Committee findings on Boeing management's response to synthetic airspeed safety proposal based on whistleblower complaint.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Bonus for meeting first flight milestone
original_label: Bonus for meeting first flight milestone

label: Production rate must be maintained
original_label: Production rate must be maintained
quote: According to the story, which was published on September 12, 2018, 'About 50 semi-finished 737s were scattered around the Renton plant last week, analysts said, several times the number of semi-finished aircraft reported in July.' The Seattle Times reported that on August 30, 2018, the Renton plant was roughly 26,600 jobs behind schedule and that this number had 'swelled' to about 31,000 jobs by the first week of September 2018, just one month after Mr. Pierson left his position at the plant. As the Seattle Times explained, 'Each job is one discrete task, each varying in complexity and the time and resources for completion.' These included items such as specific tests or installing electronics, for instance. The story seemed to validate all of the issues that Mr. Pierson had laid out for Boeing's 737 General Manager Scott Campbell and had warned him about two months earlier. One worker who spoke to the Seattle Times described the Renton plant as being in 'total chaos.' Another worker said: 'We're ripping apart some of the electronics racks already assembled to replace wire bundles that aren't right.' The Seattle Times story noted that there were lots of 'out-of-sequence work,' which Mr. Pierson had also noted, and that some workers had worked as many as nine weekends in a row without a break. Others were calling in sick just to be able to take a day off and get some rest. The Seattle Times also reported that some work groups at the plant had 'asked their managers about perhaps stopping the production lines in order to catch up' on all of the half-finished airplanes that were accumulating at the Boeing factory. 'Managers have responded categorically that a pause cannot happen because of the severe impact it would have on suppliers, on airline customers and on the company's stock price,' wrote the Seattle Times.
context: Seattle Times reporting on the Renton plant crisis, showing management rejection of production halts.

label: Production backlog and worker fatigue
original_label: Production backlog and worker fatigue
quote: In June 2018, as MAX production rates were ramping up from 47 aircraft per month to 52 aircraft per month, the problems Mr. Pierson was witnessing in the Renton plant hit a crescendo. He was concerned not just for the safety of the Boeing workforce that he managed but for the safety of the passengers who would be flying on the aircraft the Boeing factory was producing. On Saturday, June 9, 2018, at 1:32 p.m., Mr. Pierson wrote an email to Scott Campbell, the General Manager of the 737 program and the senior most official at the Renton production facility. 'Scott, I have some safety concerns that I need to share with you as the leader of the 737 Program,' wrote Mr. Pierson. 'Today we have 38 unfinished airplanes located outside the factory. The following concerns are based on my own observations and 30 years of aviation safety experience.' Mr. Pierson cited two key concerns. 'My first concern is that our workforce is exhausted. …. Fatigued employees make mistakes,' he warned. 'My second concern is schedule pressure (combined with fatigue) is creating a culture where employees are either deliberately or unconsciously circumventing established processes.'
context: Ed Pierson's email to Scott Campbell documenting production pressures and worker fatigue.

label: Military would halt for safety defects
original_label: Military would halt for safety defects

According to Mr. Pierson's testimony to the Committee in December 2019, when he walked into Mr. Campbell's office, Mr. Campbell asked him: 'Why are you here?' Mr. Pierson reminded him about their email exchange and the safety issues he had raised. Mr. Pierson recalled telling Mr. Campbell: ''In … military operations, if we have these kinds of indications of unstable safety type of things, we would stop.'' Mr. Campbell responded: ''The military is not a profit-making organization,'' according to Mr. Pierson.

label: Continue production despite safety concerns
original_label: Continue production despite safety concerns

In fact, rather than heeding Mr. Pierson's dire warnings and thoroughly evaluating his safety concerns, Boeing continued to ramp up production on the 737 MAX. Lion Air flight 610 crashed three months later.
context: Committee findings showing Boeing management's choice to continue production ramping despite documented safety concerns.

label: Pressure on MCAS training objective
original_label: Pressure on MCAS training objective

label: Chief technical pilot under pressure for Level B
original_label: Chief technical pilot under pressure for Level B

'[I]f we lose Level B,' he wrote, the blame 'will be thrown squarely on my shoulders,' conveying his feeling that he would be held personally responsible by Boeing's leadership for the financial consequences of not obtaining Level B training.

label: RCAS failure would kill MAX program
original_label: RCAS failure would kill MAX program

original_label: Boeing will not allow simulator training

original_label: Award for achieving Level B training

original_label: Simulator availability constrains training

label: Level B training target publicly announced
original_label: Level B training target publicly announced

original_label: Simulator availability limiting airline operations

label: Testing lapses and incomplete reviews
original_label: Testing lapses and incomplete reviews

label: Column cutout function modified to allow MCAS to overcome pilot elevator input
original_label: Column cutout function modified to allow MCAS to overcome pilot elevator input

When actuated, the column cutout switching modules interrupt the electrical signals to the stabilizer trim motor that are in opposition to the elevator command. The MCAS function requires the stabilizer to move nose down in opposition to the column commands when approaching high angles of attack. To accommodate MCAS, the column cutout function in the first officer's switching module was modified to inhibit the aft column cutout switch while MCAS is active, allowing Airplane nose-down stabilizer motion with Airplane nose-up column input.

The software delivered to Boeing, however, linked the AOA DISAGREE alert to the AOA position indicator, which is an optional feature on the Boeing 737 (MAX) series. Accordingly, the software activated the AOA DISAGREE alert only if an airline opted for the AOA indicator. At the time of the accident, Boeing advised that the AOA indicator hadbeen selected by approximately 20% of airlines.

original_label: Boeing determined AOA DISAGREE alert absence did not require fixing

label: MCAS functional hazard assessment did not simulate AOA sensor failure mode
original_label: MCAS functional hazard assessment did not simulate AOA sensor failure mode
quote: To perform these simulator tests, Boeing induced a stabilizer trim input that would simulate the stabilizer moving at a rate and duration consistent with the MCAS function. Boeing indicated to the NTSB that this evaluation was focused on the pilot response to uncommanded MCAS operation, regardless of underlying cause. Thus, the specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation, such as an erroneous high AOA input to the MCAS, were not simulated as part of these functional hazard assessment validation tests. As a result, additional flight deck effects (such as IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE alerts and stick shaker activation) resulting from the same underlying failure (for example, erroneous AOA) were not simulated and were not documented in the stabilizer trim and autoflight safety assessment reports reviewed by the NTSB.

label: Boeing needed MCAS to comply with control force regulations without new design

original_label: Post-reformulation sales collapse
quote: Purdue is a Delaware limited partnership that is headquartered in Stamford, Connecticut. label: Board member overrides management targets
original_label: Board member overrides management targets
quote: The executives proposed that OxyContin growth should be pegged at 3%. Richard Sackler thought this target was too low and would "lead to an OxyContin[] tablets forecast that is almost the same as our sales in 2009." A Purdue executive informed Richard Sackler that "in looking at the recent [oxycodone extended release] prescription growth trends and knowing the overall dynamics of the market OxyContin competes in – I just can't see a way of the prescription growth tracking to a level substantially higher than the 3% on which this budget is based" and that the higher target suggested by Richard Sackler would "be interpreted as an imposition as opposed to an action that will stimulate the type of business building behaviors we want to encourage." original_label: Federal healthcare programs as revenue driver

original_label: Significant budget shortfall after reformulation

label: Board revised forecast downward
original_label: Board revised forecast downward

label: Board member demands corrective actions
original_label: Board member demands corrective actions

label: Board calls for CEO and sales head replacement
original_label: Board calls for CEO and sales head replacement

label: OxyContin sales below budget multiple years
original_label: OxyContin sales below budget multiple years

original_label: Decision to intensify targeting high-volume prescribers

original_label: Board sets ambitious OxyContin growth targets

context: In January 2010, Richard Sackler communicated to the Board that OxyContin and other oxycodone extended release products were the critical driver of the firm's overall sales growth, establishing them as strategic targets.

original_label: Executive explains market reality constraints
quote: A Purdue executive informed Richard Sackler that "in looking at the recent [oxycodone extended release] prescription growth trends and knowing the overall dynamics of the market OxyContin competes in – I just can't see a way of the prescription growth tracking to a level substantially higher than the 3% on which this budget is based"

original_label: High-volume prescriber losses attributed to abuse controls

original_label: Decision to re-enable detailing of flagged prescribers

label: Board briefing on abuse shift from injection to oral
original_label: Board briefing on abuse shift from injection to oral

The study examined a two-year period, August 2009 to July 2011, and found that data for Region Zero prescribers showed an 86% decline in their OxyContin prescriptions after Purdue's introduction of its reformulated version, and especially at the highest dosages, 40 and 80 mg tablets. The study found that prescribers suspected of abuse and diversion also prescribed the highest dose (80 mg) of OxyContin more frequently than other prescribers. The study also found that Region Zero prescribers accounted for only 38.4% of the overall decline in sales post-reformulation, which Purdue attributed to reduced abuse of OxyContin. The remaining 61.6% of the decline was among other prescribers that were not on Purdue's Region Zero lists, meaning that sales representatives either were continuing to call on these prescribers or were permitted to do so.
context: The Board received analysis showing that 61.6% of post-reformulation OxyContin decline came from non-Region Zero prescribers whom Purdue sales reps were still detailing, indicating Purdue knowingly chose to continue marketing to a large group of remaining high-volume prescribers despite recognizing they were losing abuse-related revenues.

label: Board learns abuse shifted to oral ingestion route
original_label: Board learns abuse shifted to oral ingestion route
quote: The study also found that immediate-release oxycodone prescribing increased at a similar rate (an approximately 32% increase) to the decline in 80 mg and 40 mg tablets of Reformulated OxyContin prescriptions (which experienced a 24% decrease and 26% decrease, respectively) among the non-Region Zero comparator prescribers, indicating that patients who had been abusing OxyContin may have been shifted to a non-reformulated oxycodone product that they could continue to misuse. Versions of the presentation, including at least one provided to Richard Sackler in August 2013, repeated key findings, including: "Greater declines for doctors that were potentially problematic prescribers"; "Greater declines for high versus low dosage strengths"; "A small number of prescribers contribute to a large proportion of potential diversion of opioids from legal to illegal channels"; and "there were doctors in the [Purdue's] database who were prescribing painkillers 'for what appears to be the wrong reasons.'"

label: Safeguards from law enforcement and retail chains
original_label: Safeguards from law enforcement and retail chains

original_label: Consultant identifies pharmacy access as barrier

context: In 2013, external consultants informed Purdue's Board that traditional pharmacy and wholesale channels were implementing hard access controls that blocked OxyContin prescriptions from reaching patients, making legitimate distribution channels unavailable for revenue recovery.

label: Decision to turbocharge sales through E2E
original_label: Decision to turbocharge sales through E2E

original_label: E2E proposal focuses on extreme high-volume prescribers

original_label: Board receives E2E implementation plan

label: E2E targets extreme high-volume prescribers with increased frequency
original_label: E2E targets extreme high-volume prescribers with increased frequency

label: E2E call frequency targets for top prescribers
original_label: E2E call frequency targets for top prescribers
quote: Based on a study showing that providers in deciles 7-10 were most responsive to sales calls and were the most prolific writers, the E2E call plans instructed sales representatives to call on the very highest deciles of high-volume prescribers (i.e., those in so-called "deciles" 7 through 10) at least 24 times a year and "heavily favor" promoting OxyContin over other Purdue opioids in their messaging. label: Sales messaging designed to increase titration
original_label: Sales messaging designed to increase titration

label: Scripts override safety concerns about addiction
original_label: Scripts override safety concerns about addiction
