Specifically, representatives were trained to pivot from legitimate physician concerns about addiction to statements about "dependence" and opioid "tolerance." When asked about the safety of high dosages, representatives were instructed to respond that OxyContin "does not have a ceiling dose."
context: Purdue training scripts instructed sales representatives to reframe physician safety concerns about addiction as issues of dependence and tolerance, and to counter concerns about high-dose safety by stating OxyContin has no ceiling dose, enabling reps to overcome prescriber resistance to increased prescriptions.

label: Board recognizes pharmacy refusal of prescriptions
original_label: Board recognizes pharmacy refusal of prescriptions
quote: The Board received information concerning "OxyContin strength Rx history as well as statistical projections" that attributed the decline in sales of the high dosage tablets to "DEA pressures and 'good faith dispensing policies' at large chain pharmacies, fewer patients switching into the ERO market from other products, and there are fewer patients titrating to the higher strengths from the lower ones" (emphasis in original).
context: The Board was informed that pharmacy good-faith dispensing policies were blocking OxyContin high-dose prescriptions, establishing that pharmacies were actively refusing to fill orders they deemed medically unnecessary.

label: Board approved pharmacy detailing strategy
original_label: Board approved pharmacy detailing strategy
quote: At the November 2013 meeting concerning Purdue's 2014 budget, a Purdue executive discussed with the Board the company's plan to "refine the message" of the company's titration up marketing campaign and specifically referenced the "Individualize the Dose" campaign, a Conversion & Titration Guide, and the S.T.A.R.T. principles to "highlight important elements of titration throughout the course of treatment."
context: In November 2013, the Board approved refinement of titration-up messaging and specifically endorsed campaigns to push higher dosages and discourage patient switches away from OxyContin.

label: Region Zero list contains abuse/diversion indicators
original_label: Region Zero list contains abuse/diversion indicators
quote: At all relevant times, Purdue maintained an ADD program, through which Purdue had the means and ability to identify prescribers suspected of engaging in abuse and diversion. The ADD program began in or around 2002 and ended in or around February 2018. It was governed during most of that time period by Standard Operating Procedure ("SOP") 1.7.1. SOP 1.7.1 instructed Purdue employees to refer prescribers who displayed indicia of abuse and diversion to ADD. Employees referred these prescribers to ADD by issuing a Report of Concern ("ROC"). The indicia of abuse and diversion in SOP 1.7.1 were amended over time and included, among other things, excessive numbers of patients; brief or nonexistent contact with patients; high numbers of cash pay patients; information that a prescriber or his or her patients may be diverting opioids; allegations of patient overdoses; allegations of unauthorized individuals signing prescriptions; large numbers of patients traveling long distances; and allegations that a prescriber is under investigation.
context: Purdue maintained a detailed ADD program with criteria for identifying prescribers showing abuse and diversion red flags, but this system operated independently from and did not override E2E's targeting of high-volume prescribers despite overlap.

label: Purdue continued detailing flagged prescribers
original_label: Purdue continued detailing flagged prescribers
quote: Purdue was aware that Region Zero providers were responsible for a major drop in sales after Reformulated OxyContin was released, and that there were also declines among prescribers that were not on Region Zero that Purdue sales representatives could continue to detail. Purdue sales representatives were trained to report prescribers suspected of abuse and diversion to ADD, and some sales representatives did so. However, high-volume prescribers were often not reported and, even if they were, they were sometimes not added to Region Zero until they lost the ability to prescribe through legal or medical board action. In addition, certain Purdue policies resulted in high-volume prescribers not being reported to ADD, and thus not being added to Region Zero. For example, Purdue trained its sales representatives to only report clear instances of abuse and diversion, and sales representatives were instructed to discuss the reports with their district managers prior to filing. In addition, although Purdue's policy stated that it required timely reporting, Purdue had few, if any, effective compliance measures to address an employee's failure to report, and very few sales representatives were penalized for failing to timely report.
context: Despite having an ADD program to identify abuse-diversion risk prescribers, Purdue deliberately structured its reporting processes to keep high-volume prescribers off Region Zero lists, allowing continued detailing of suspected bad actors who remained valuable to the firm.

label: Purdue permitted sales rep petitions to reinstate flagged prescribers
original_label: Purdue permitted sales rep petitions to reinstate flagged prescribers
quote: Further, even for those prescribers who were placed on Region Zero, Purdue engaged in other practices to increase those prescribers' opioid prescriptions. Purdue permitted sales representatives to continue calling on other members of the exact same practice, although doing so could increase the prescriptions of the Region Zero prescriber; Purdue detailed its highest-volume prescribers' pharmacies in order to increase the likelihood that Region Zero prescriptions would be filled; and Purdue permitted sales representatives and managers to petition to have Region Zero status reversed so they could resume calling on Region Zero prescribers. These petitions were sometimes granted. For example, in 2012, Purdue employees petitioned for over 180 mid to high-decile Region Zero providers to be reinstated.
context: Even when prescribers were placed on Region Zero for abuse/diversion concerns, Purdue systematically granted requests from sales reps to reinstate them, petitioning to remove over 180 high-volume prescribers in 2012 alone, prioritizing revenue over safety flags.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Prescribers paid for speaking based on volume
original_label: Prescribers paid for speaking based on volume
quote: Purdue allowed its sales and marketing personnel, who had data on each doctor's prescribing of Purdue's drugs and whose compensation depended on increasing their assigned doctors' prescribing of Purdue's drugs, to select speakers instead of Purdue's medical education staff. Purdue also allowed its sales representatives to relay and endorse doctors' requests to be retained, and the doctors could be selected even if they had not been identified by the consulting company Purdue had retained for this purpose. Within Purdue, these were known as "unsolicited requests." Purdue vested final authority to select doctors in Purdue's Marketing department, which had data on each doctor's Purdue prescriptions.
context: Purdue gave its sales and marketing staff—compensated on prescription volumes—authority to select which doctors would be paid as speakers, creating a direct financial incentive to select high-prescribing doctors for speaker fees regardless of their medical legitimacy.

label: Kickback payments to high-volume prescribers
original_label: Kickback payments to high-volume prescribers
quote: Purdue paid the highest-volume OxyContin prescriber in the United States over $160,000 between 2013 and May 2018 because he was, in the words of Purdue's employees, "the biggest prescriber in CT," "the #3 prescriber of opioids nationally," and "very important to our success," even after he indicated that if he stopped receiving speaking assignments from Purdue, "the love may be lost." Purdue paid the highest-volume OxyContin prescriber in Medicare approximately $475,000 between 2013 and January 2017 to deliver speeches and advice even though Purdue observed he was "not a strong speaker or presenter" and "attendees couldn't follow him," he engaged in "heavy prescribing, particularly in large doses for long periods of time," and was excluded by Florida Medicaid. Purdue paid more than $110,000 to a high-volume prescriber who demanded speaking assignments or else he would "re-evaluate the use of [Purdue's] products."
context: Purdue made substantial payments to top-volume prescribers for speaking despite knowing they were not effective speakers and in some cases only to prevent those prescribers from reducing their OxyContin prescribing—clear evidence of kickbacks tied to prescription volume.

label: Practice Fusion kickback for EHR prescribing prompts
original_label: Practice Fusion kickback for EHR prescribing prompts
quote: Beginning in or around spring 2014, Purdue discussed paying Practice Fusion to create a CDS alert ("Pain CDS") to prompt providers using Practice Fusion's EHR to take certain clinical actions that Purdue believed would increase prescriptions for Purdue's extended release opioid products ("EROs"), which included OxyContin, Butrans, and Hysingla. From the beginning, the primary purpose of the program was to increase Purdue's ERO prescriptions. On May 4, 2014, a Purdue executive wrote regarding a potential deal with Practice Fusion that "[t]he key is understanding how it grows or protects [prescriptions]."
context: Purdue designed a kickback scheme with Practice Fusion, explicitly structured from inception to increase OxyContin prescriptions, in which Purdue paid nearly $1 million for EHR software alerts to prompt prescribers to write more opioid prescriptions.

label: Purdue approved prescription-increasing CDS alert design
original_label: Purdue approved prescription-increasing CDS alert design
quote: Purdue participated in the design of the Pain CDS alert. It approved the types of patients the Pain CDS would target and what guidance the alert would provide healthcare providers. The Pain CDS was presented to providers as a neutral medical standard. However, Purdue's primary objective in designing of the CDS alert was to increase its ERO sales,-and the Pain CDS deviated from medically accepted standards, CDC guidelines, and FDA-approved labels for Purdue's EROs.
context: Purdue directly controlled the design of the Practice Fusion CDS alert to maximize prescription generation, deliberately misrepresenting it as a neutral medical tool while departing from CDC guidelines and FDA labeling to serve Purdue's sales objectives.

label: Sacklers approved alternative pharmacy distribution
original_label: Sacklers approved alternative pharmacy distribution
quote: As an additional means to circumvent safeguards intended to prevent the filling of suspicious prescriptions, from October 2015 through 2018, Purdue and certain of the Sacklers sought to find a pharmacy mechanism to fill OxyContin prescriptions that other traditional pharmacies had rejected. As noted above, in July 2013, as part of the E2E program, the consulting company relayed to Purdue and the Board that OxyContin revenues were down because, among other things, "entire pharmacies [are] being shut off by distributors, pharmacies themselves imposing tablet limits, decreases in channel inventory leading to greater stockouts, and pharmacies choosing to not stock OxyContin."
context: Facing rejection of OxyContin prescriptions by traditional pharmacies implementing safeguards, Purdue and the Sacklers developed an alternative distribution strategy beginning in 2015 to fill prescriptions that legitimate pharmacies had refused.

label: Sacklers propose specialized distribution bypass
original_label: Sacklers propose specialized distribution bypass
quote: On August 16, 2013, one day after the Board briefing on E2E discussed above, Mortimer D. A. Sackler emailed a Purdue executive and others asking what ideas management had for creating a new distribution system "to help relieve this problem of product access for legitimate chronic pain patients," which would use "an independent service to verify the legitimacy of [the patients'] prescriptions." Two days later, Mortimer D.A. Sackler reiterated, "I do think there may be an opportunity here for us to set up a complimentary business to handle this for Purdue as well as other controlled drug manufacturers. Do we have a team who could explore this possibility?" On August 18, 2013, Richard Sackler responded that he had the same idea and expressed it to a Purdue executive after a Board meeting. That Purdue executive responded three days later confirming Mortimer D.A. Sackler's interest in exploring an "alternative distribution process for all or essentially all opioid formulations." Mortimer D.A. Sackler responded on the same day, "To be clear, I was thinking about selling to pharmacies."
context: In August 2013, Sackler family members actively proposed creating an alternative distribution mechanism outside traditional pharmacy channels to circumvent the access barriers that legitimate pharmacies had erected to block suspect OxyContin prescriptions.

label: Specialty pharmacy agreements to fill rejected prescriptions
original_label: Specialty pharmacy agreements to fill rejected prescriptions
quote: Shortly thereafter, the Sacklers approved E2E, and the E2E program went on to develop "multiple tactics to address these issues," including "alternative supply channels." In 2015, the Company entered agreements with three specialty pharmacies. Some of the prescriptions that were filled by the specialty pharmacies had been rejected by traditional retail pharmacies and displayed indicia that the prescriptions were not for a medically accepted indication; for uses that were unsafe, ineffective, and medically unnecessary; and that were often diverted for uses that lacked a legitimate medical purpose. Purdue's ADD program data further confirms that some of these prescriptions lacked medical necessity. From mid-2015 through 2018, the specialty pharmacies filled Medicare prescriptions for Purdue opioids written by approximately 100 prescribers. Nearly one-fourth of those prescribers were referred to ADD on suspicion of engaging in abuse and diversion.
context: In 2015, following Sackler approval, Purdue entered agreements with specialty pharmacies to fill prescriptions that traditional pharmacies had rejected, and nearly 25% of the prescribers using these pharmacies had been flagged by Purdue's own ADD program for suspected abuse and diversion.

label: Purdue paid specialty pharmacies above fair market value
original_label: Purdue paid specialty pharmacies above fair market value
quote: From October 2015 through 2018, Purdue paid the specialty pharmacies over $100,000 in kickbacks to fill prescriptions that other traditional pharmacies had rejected. By October 2013 and in connection with Purdue's alternative distribution model strategies, Purdue had approached six potential partners, but all six rejected Purdue's offer because they were "not comfortable with mail fulfillment" and were concerned with the "risk associated with dispensing OxyContin" under that model. The agreements Purdue ultimately entered into with three specialty pharmacies made payments at above fair market value that were tied to the volume of Hysingla the pharmacy dispensed.
context: Purdue paid specialty pharmacies over $100,000 in volume-based fees above fair market value starting in October 2015 to fill OxyContin and other opioids that traditional pharmacies had refused, after six other potential partners rejected the arrangement due to safety concerns.

label: Credit rating and financial statement targets
original_label: Credit rating and financial statement targets
quote: In order to ensure an investment-grade credit rating, Enron began to emphasize increasing its cash flow, lowering its debt, and smoothing its earnings on its financial statements to meet the criteria set by credit rating agencies like Moody's and Standard & Poor's.
context: Senate report describing Enron's stated business strategy during the 1990s.

label: Asset light strategy and syndication requirements
original_label: Asset light strategy and syndication requirements
quote: A presentation made to the Finance Committee in October 2000, summarized this strategy as follows. It stated that Enron's '[e]nergy and communications investments typically do not generate significant cashflow and earnings for 1 to 3 years.' It stated that Enron had '[l]imited cash flow to service additional debt' and '[l]imited earnings to cover dilution of additional equity.' It concluded that 'Enron must syndicate' or share its investment costs 'in order to grow.'
context: Senate report quoting Enron Finance Committee presentation establishing asset syndication as organizational imperative.

label: Board set funds flow and balance sheet targets
original_label: Board set funds flow and balance sheet targets
quote: The Board itself apparently set 'funds flow and balance sheet ratio targets' for Enron to achieve, as shown by an Enron Global Markets presentation reporting on the company's actual versus targeted performance.
context: Senate report analyzing documents showing Board-level establishment of specific financial metrics.

label: 64 percent of assets troubled or underperforming
original_label: 64 percent of assets troubled or underperforming
quote: In April, Board members were told that 64 percent of Enron's assets were 'troubled' or performing 'below expectations.' They were also told of international assets that were overvalued on Enron's books by $2.3 billion.
context: Senate report summarizing 2001 Finance Committee briefing to Board on deteriorating asset portfolio.

label: Stock price decline and market skepticism in 2001
original_label: Stock price decline and market skepticism in 2001
quote: In 2001, evidence began to mount that not all was well at Enron. The company's stock price began declining. In March 2001, a prominent Fortune article questioned the company's opaque financial statements.
context: Senate report chronicling early 2001 warning signs of financial distress.

label: Gross revenues jumped from 40 billion to 100 billion in one year
original_label: Gross revenues jumped from 40 billion to 100 billion in one year
quote: The Board was also informed that, in 6 short months, LJM had produced over $2 billion in funds flow for Enron, and Enron's gross revenues had jumped from $40 billion in 1999 to $100 billion in 2000. These figures are striking, yet apparently no Board member questioned them.
context: Senate report noting Board's awareness of dramatic revenue increase and LJM performance without apparent scrutiny.

label: Problem of finding independent counterparties for assets
original_label: Problem of finding independent counterparties for assets
quote: One of the problems with Enron's new strategies, however, was finding counterparties willing to invest in Enron assets or share the significant risks associated with long-term energy production facilities and delivery contracts.
context: Senate report explaining structural impediment to Enron's asset syndication strategy using legitimate third parties.

label: Enron's focus on credit rating maintenance
original_label: Enron's focus on credit rating maintenance
quote: All of the Board members interviewed by the Subcommittee were well aware of and supported Enron's intense focus on its credit rating, cash flow, and debt burden.
context: Senate report summarizing Board's collective awareness of Enron's strategic preoccupation with maintaining credit metrics.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: CEO compensation exceeding 140 million in 2000
original_label: CEO compensation exceeding 140 million in 2000
quote: In 2000, Mr. Lay's total compensation exceeded $140 million, including $123 million from exercising a portion of his Enron stock options, an amount which exceeded average CEO pay at U.S. publicly traded corporations by a factor of ten and made him one of the highest paid CEOs in the country.
context: Senate report documenting Chairman and CEO Kenneth Lay's compensation structure tied to stock price appreciation.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: 430 million in annual bonuses plus 320 million performance unit bonuses
original_label: 430 million in annual bonuses plus 320 million performance unit bonuses
quote: That year, Enron executives received about $430 million in annual bonuses under Enron's normal bonus plan. In addition, in exchange for meeting certain stock performance targets, a special program called the Performance Unit Plan paid bonuses to about 65 Enron executives totaling another $320 million. Board members indicated that they had been unaware that the company had paid out almost $750 million in cash bonuses for a year in which the company's entire net income was $975 million.
context: Senate report showing massive bonus payments to executives tied to performance targets, unknown to Board in aggregate.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Lou Pai accumulated 265 million from stock option exercise
original_label: Lou Pai accumulated 265 million from stock option exercise
quote: One executive, Lou Pai, accumulated enough stock options that, when he exercised them and sold the underlying stock in 2000, he left the company with more than $265 million in cash.
context: Senate report documenting individual executive wealth accumulation from stock options.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Stock-based compensation created incentives to manipulate earnings
original_label: Stock-based compensation created incentives to manipulate earnings
quote: During their interviews, the Committee members said it had not occurred to them that, by giving Enron executives huge stock option awards, they might be creating incentives for Enron executives to improperly manipulate company earnings to increase the company stock price and cash in their options.
context: Senate report noting Board's lack of awareness that compensation structure incentivized accounting manipulation.

label: Board waived ethics code to allow CFO to operate LJM partnerships
original_label: Board waived ethics code to allow CFO to operate LJM partnerships
quote: In the case of the LJM partnerships, Mr. Lay approved waiving the code of conduct prohibition for Mr. Fastow, but also asked the Enron Board to ratify his decision, even though Board concurrence was not explicitly required by company rules. Evidence introduced in the Andersen criminal trial indicates that the idea for Board ratification may have originated with Andersen.
context: Senate report documenting Board's approval of unprecedented code of conduct waiver for CFO.

label: Andersen partners expressed alarm at LJM conflict of interest
original_label: Andersen partners expressed alarm at LJM conflict of interest
quote: Apparently, a number of senior Andersen personnel, including David Duncan, had serious concerns about the LJM proposal and were reluctant to support it. Benjamin Neuhausen, a member of Andersen's Professional Standard Group, wrote in a 5/28/99 email to David Duncan: 'Setting aside the accounting, idea of a venture entity managed by CFO is terrible from a business point of view. Conflicts galore. Why would any director in his or her right mind ever approve such a scheme?'
context: Senate report quoting Andersen internal email expressing deep concerns about LJM structure that Board nonetheless approved.

label: Andersen required Board approval and CEO involvement for LJM support
original_label: Andersen required Board approval and CEO involvement for LJM support
quote: Mr. Duncan responded in a 6/1/99 email as follows: '[O]n your point 1 (i.e., the whole thing is a bad idea), I really couldn't agree more. Rest assured that I have already communicated and it has been agreed to by Andy that CEO, General [Counsel], and Board discussion and approval will be a requirement, on our part, for acceptance of a venture similar to what we have been discussing.'
context: Senate report quoting Andersen partner response conditioning firm's support of LJM on Board ratification.

label: Purpose of Raptor transactions was accounting protection not economic hedging
original_label: Purpose of Raptor transactions was accounting protection not economic hedging
quote: A handwritten note taken by the Corporate Secretary during Committee consideration of the Raptors states: 'Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P&L volatility.' The final page lists three risks associated with the Raptors. The first risk is 'Accounting scrutiny'; the second is 'Substantial decline in the price of [Enron] stock'; and the third is 'Counterparty credit.' The Raptor I presentation contains all the information necessary for a Board of 'experts in areas of finance and accounting,' as Mr. Duncan described his fellow Board members, to understand that the Raptor transactions were designed to function, not as a true hedge, but rather as an accounting gimmick whose sole purpose was to improve Enron's financial statements.
context: Senate report analyzing Finance Committee presentation showing Board was told Raptors transferred P&L volatility without economic risk transfer.

label: Raptors used Enron stock collateral to offset investment losses
original_label: Raptors used Enron stock collateral to offset investment losses
quote: The Powers Report described them as an improper attempt by Enron to use the value of its own stock to offset losses in its investment portfolio, and 'a highly complex accounting construct that was destined to collapse.' In each of the Raptor transactions, Enron orchestrated the establishment of a special purpose entity (SPE) and arranged for LJM2 to provide the SPE with $30 million which Enron deemed, with Andersen's concurrence, to be the independent equity from a third party needed to qualify the SPE for separate accounting treatment from Enron. Enron explicitly assured LJM2 that it would recoup its money plus an additional $10 million within 6 months of each SPE's establishment. Enron then arranged for the Raptor SPEs to appear to hedge millions of dollars in volatile investments held by Enron, and made the SPEs appear to be creditworthy on paper—despite withdrawal of the LJM funds—by pledging as collateral hundreds of millions of dollars worth of Enron's stock, contracts to buy Enron stock in the future, or warrants to buy stock in a related company called The New Power Company (TNPC).
context: Senate report explaining structure of Raptor transactions approved by Board as means to conceal investment losses.

label: Raptors concealed 1 billion in investment losses
original_label: Raptors concealed 1 billion in investment losses
quote: Enron claimed, again with Andersen's concurrence, that it could use the so-called Raptor hedges to offset mounting losses in its investments which Enron otherwise would have had to report on its income statement and subtract from its earnings. In the space of 1 year, Enron used the alleged Raptor hedges to offset—or, in the words of the Powers Report, 'conceal from the market'—losses of almost $1 billion.
context: Senate report describing how Raptor transactions functioned to mask investment portfolio deterioration.

label: Off-balance-sheet strategy to improve financial appearance
original_label: Off-balance-sheet strategy to improve financial appearance
quote: Enron's multi-billion dollar, off-the-books activity was disclosed to the Enron Board and received Board approval as an explicit strategy to improve Enron's financial statements. In fact, Enron's massive off-the-books activity could not have taken place without Board action to establish new special purpose entities, issue preferred Enron shares, and pledge Enron stock as the collateral needed for the deals to go forward. In the end, the Board knowingly allowed Enron to move at least $27 billion or almost 50 percent of its assets off-balance-sheet.
context: Senate report summarizing Board's explicit authorization of off-balance-sheet strategy to enhance financial statements.

label: Whitewing moved off books while pledging Enron stock as collateral
original_label: Whitewing moved off books while pledging Enron stock as collateral
quote: In September 1999, the Board approved a resolution to restructure Whitewing as an 'unconsolidated affiliate' that could be removed from Enron's books. At the same time, the Board approved establishment of a special purpose entity called the Osprey Trust to invest in Whitewing, and authorized Osprey to issue $1.4 billion in debt instruments that could be secured by a second series of Enron preferred shares. By taking this action, the Board simultaneously moved Whitewing off Enron's balance sheet, while pledging Enron stock to secure Whitewing's debt. These debt instruments were subsequently sold to investors as bonds paying an 8 percent return, collateralized with Enron stock. Whitewing then used the funds to purchase Enron assets, injecting substantial cash into Enron which, in turn, reported that cash on its financial statements as funds flow from asset sales and investments.
context: Senate report documenting Board's deliberate restructuring of Whitewing to remove assets from balance sheet while securing debt with Enron stock.

label: LJM transactions designed to book earnings and funds flow
original_label: LJM transactions designed to book earnings and funds flow
quote: Like Whitewing, LJM1 and LJM2 were explicitly established and run by Enron personnel. Unlike Whitewing, the LJM partnerships were set up from the beginning to function as off-the-books entities intended to transact business with Enron and improve Enron's financial statements. Over the course of 2 years, Enron entered into over two dozen transactions with LJM1 and LJM2 involving hundreds of millions of dollars. LJM1's first transaction, which was presented to and approved by the Board at its June 1999 meeting, was the Rhythms stock 'hedge' whose sole purpose was to protect Enron's income statement from loss if the stock were to drop in price. The first seven LJM2 transactions, all of which took place in 1999, consisted of Enron's selling poorly performing assets to LJM2, which enabled Enron to move debt off its books and show inflated earnings and cash flow from the asset sales on its 1999 financial statements.
context: Senate report describing deliberate design of LJM partnerships to generate favorable accounting and financial statement treatment.

label: Andersen knew Enron used high-risk accounting practices
original_label: Andersen knew Enron used high-risk accounting practices
quote: Andersen's 1999 and 2000 client risk analyses placed Enron in its category for 'Maximum' risk. The 2000 analysis, which was signed by David Duncan and four other Andersen partners, identified several 'Risk Drivers' for Enron, including stating that Enron 'Management Pressures' were 'Very Significant' and that the 'Accounting and Financial Reporting Risk' associated with Enron was also 'Very Significant.' The analyses offered some specific comments explaining the maximum risk rating, including the following: 'Enron has aggressive earnings targets and enters into numerous complex transactions to achieve those targets.' 'The Company's personnel are very sophisticated and enter into numerous complex transactions and are often aggressive in structuring transactions to achieve derived financial reporting objectives.' 'Form over substance transactions.'
context: Senate report citing Andersen's own internal risk analyses showing recognition of aggressive transaction structuring to achieve earnings targets.

label: Board approved high-risk accounting practices knowingly
original_label: Board approved high-risk accounting practices knowingly
quote: On February 7, 1999, Andersen informed the Audit Committee members that Enron was engaged in accounting practices that 'push limits' or were 'at the edge' of acceptable practice. In the discussion that followed, Andersen did not advocate any change in company practice, and no Board member objected to Enron's actions, requested a second opinion of Enron's accounting practices, or demanded a more prudent approach.
context: Senate report documenting Board's knowing acceptance of high-risk accounting despite Andersen's explicit warnings.

label: Duncan's handwritten note: practices push limits and have high risk profile
original_label: Duncan's handwritten note: practices push limits and have high risk profile
quote: A handwritten note by Mr. Duncan in the lower right-hand corner of the document states: 'Obviously, we are on board with all of these, but many push limits and have a high 'others could have a different view' risk profile.' While Mr. Duncan did not make himself available in response to a Subcommittee request to elaborate on this note, his colleague Mr. Bauer confirmed through legal counsel that Mr. Duncan had conveyed this information to the Audit Committee.
context: Senate report quoting Andersen engagement partner's contemporaneous assessment of Enron's accounting practices pushing acceptable limits.

label: Inadequate disclosure of off-the-books liabilities
original_label: Inadequate disclosure of off-the-books liabilities
quote: When asked about Enron's extensive off-the-books activity, one of the Board members, Mr. Blake, stated during his interview that transferring assets off a company's books 'is not immoral as long as disclosed.' But here, too, the Enron Board failed in its fiduciary duty to ensure adequate public disclosure of Enron's off-the-books assets and liabilities. Enron's initial public disclosures regarding its dealings with its 'unconsolidated affiliates' such as JEDI, Whitewing, LJM, and the Raptor SPEs are nearly impossible to understand and difficult to reconcile with the transactions now known to have taken place. The Powers Report calls the disclosures 'fundamentally inadequate' and castigates Enron for proxy statement and financial statement disclosures that fail to 'disclose facts that were important for an understanding of the substance of the transactions' Enron entered into with related parties.
context: Senate report analyzing Board's failure to ensure adequate public disclosure of related-party transactions and off-balance-sheet structures.

label: Watkins warned accounting would not survive daylight scrutiny
original_label: Watkins warned accounting would not survive daylight scrutiny
quote: Ms. Watkins also focused on the lack of adequate public disclosure of the company's involvement in the Raptor transactions in her August 2001 letter to Mr. Lay. Her letter states that 'a lot of smart people' are examining the Raptor transactions and 'a lot of accountants including [Andersen] have blessed the accounting treatment. None of that will protect Enron if these transactions are ever disclosed in the bright light of day.' The letter continues: 'The overriding principle of accounting is that if you explain the accounting treatment to a man on the street, would you influence his investing decisions? Would he buy or sell the stock based on a thorough understanding of the facts? If so, you best present it correctly and/or change the accounting. My concern is that the footnotes don't adequately explain the transactions. If adequately explained, the investor would know that the Entities described in our related party footnote are thinly capitalized, the equity holders have no skin in the game, and all the value in the entities comes from the underlying value of the derivatives (unfortunately in this case, a big loss) AND Enron stock and N/P.'
context: Senate report quoting whistleblower Sherron Watkins' August 2001 letter warning of inadequate disclosure and accounting that would not withstand scrutiny.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Lay used credit line 77 million in one year via stock repayment
original_label: Lay used credit line 77 million in one year via stock repayment
quote: In the 1-year period from October 2000 to October 2001, Mr. Lay used the credit line to obtain over $77 million in cash from the company and repaid the loans exclusively with Enron stock. Several directors confirmed that Mr. Lay still owed the company about $7 million. The interviewed Board members said they had been unaware of these transactions at the time and agreed that they could fairly be characterized as stock sales. They indicated that they had been unaware at the time that, by characterizing the stock transfers as loan payments rather than stock sales, Mr. Lay bypassed requirements for reporting insider stock sales on a quarterly basis and instead delayed reporting the transactions to the SEC and investing public until the end of the calendar year in which they took place.
context: Senate report documenting CEO's use of company credit line to obtain cash repaid with discounted stock, with reporting implications.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Board compensation package 350000 annually above market norms
original_label: Board compensation package 350000 annually above market norms
quote: Enron Board members were compensated with cash, restricted stock, phantom stock units, and stock options. The total cash and equity compensation of Enron Board members in 2000 was valued by Enron at about $350,000 or more than twice the national average for Board compensation at a U.S. publicly traded corporation.
context: Senate report documenting Board compensation structure tied to stock appreciation that exceeded market norms.

label: LJM partnerships realized hundreds of millions in profits at Enron expense
original_label: LJM partnerships realized hundreds of millions in profits at Enron expense
quote: The Enron Board approved code of conduct waivers for Mr. Fastow knowing that the LJM partnerships were designed to transact business primarily with Enron, and controls would be needed to ensure the LJM transactions and Mr. Fastow's compensation were fair to Enron. The Board failed, however, to make sure the controls were effective, to monitor the fairness of the transactions, or to monitor Mr. Fastow's LJM-related compensation. The result was that the LJM partnerships realized hundreds of millions of dollars in profits at Enron's expense.
context: Senate report summarizing Board's approval of LJM structure knowing it would generate related-party profits.

label: Fastow received 45 million from LJM in two years on 5 million investment
original_label: Fastow received 45 million from LJM in two years on 5 million investment
quote: Mr. Fastow told the Board that he had earned $45 million on a $5 million investment in LJM1 and LJM2 in just 2 years. Other Enron employees also admitted to significant LJM returns in a short period, including two who received immediate returns of $1 million each on individual investments of $5,800.

original_label: SMS procedures remain separate from legacy safety systems

original_label: Disconnect between senior and mid-level safety culture

original_label: Employees skeptical about SMS program sustainability

original_label: Boeing treated SMS as audit compliance rather than culture change

label: Human factors expertise eroded and not easily rebuilt
original_label: Human factors expertise eroded and not easily rebuilt

original_label: SMS messaging inconsistent across worksites and employee groups

original_label: SMS implemented as regulatory compliance checklist

original_label: ODA unit members at non-Renton sites feel unsupported

original_label: FAA management overruled UM decisions without consultation

original_label: Boeing attempted to maintain legacy and SMS systems in parallel

label: Defeat device installed to circumvent emissions standards
original_label: Defeat device installed to circumvent emissions standards

context: EPA director Christopher Grundler testifying to Congress on October 8, 2015, describing the core technical choice VW made to achieve emissions compliance in testing while violating standards in actual use.

label: Defeat device mechanism and emissions exceedance
original_label: Defeat device mechanism and emissions exceedance
quote: Known as a "defeat device," this design feature results in the cars emitting up to 40 times the emissions that are allowed to ensure public health is protected. These devices contain a "switch" that senses whether the vehicle is being tested or not based on various inputs, including the position of the steering wheel, vehicle speed, the duration of the engine's operation, and barometric pressure.
context: EPA testimony explaining the technical specifics of how the defeat device functioned to enable massive emissions violations while passing certification tests.

label: Misrepresentation to EPA and concealment of violations
original_label: Misrepresentation to EPA and concealment of violations

These violations are very serious. Not only because the illegal defeat device results in excess emissions many times the allowable standard, but also because after the high emissions were discovered, VW concealed the facts from the EPA, the State of California, and from consumers.
context: EPA testimony characterizing the violation as involving both the initial deception through false certification and subsequent concealment of the misconduct.

label: No greater than Level B training objective
original_label: No greater than Level B training objective
quote: Principally for this reason, Boeing's stated objectives in designing the 737 MAX included securing the FAA AEG's determination to require no greater than "Level B" differences training in the 737 MAX FSB Report. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 understood as much. For example, in or around November 2014, Boeing Employee-2 wrote in an internal Boeing electronic chat communication to Boeing Employee-1 that "nothing can jepordize [sic] level b[.]" In or around December 2014, Boeing Employee-1 wrote in an email to another Boeing employee that "if we lose Level B [it] will be thrown squarely on my shoulders. It was [Boeing Employee-1], yes [Boeing Employee-1]! Who cost Boeing tens of millions of dollars!"
context: Statement of Facts describing Boeing's explicit goal to secure Level B training rather than Level D, tied to financial impact on the 737 MAX program and individual accountability.

label: Fuel efficiency and competitive advantage against Airbus
original_label: Fuel efficiency and competitive advantage against Airbus
quote: In or around June 2011, Boeing began developing and marketing a new version of its Boeing 737 called the 737 MAX. The 737 MAX was designed by Boeing as a competitive answer to a new version of an airplane developed by one of Boeing's top rivals in commercial airplanes, Company-1. Like the new version of Company-1's airplane, the 737 MAX promised increased fuel efficiency over its prior version, the 737 Next Generation ("737 NG"). With this increased efficiency, the 737 MAX offered fuel-cost savings for airlines.
context: Statement of Facts explaining the market context and competitive pressure driving the 737 MAX design as a response to Airbus.

label: Level B reduces pilot training costs for customers
original_label: Level B reduces pilot training costs for customers
quote: As Boeing knew, "Level B" differences training was significantly less expensive for airlines to complete than "Level D." For example, a pilot could complete "Level B" differences training from anywhere in the world in a matter of hours using a computer or tablet. In contrast, a pilot could complete "Level D" differences training only by appearing in person wherever the pilot's airline operated a full-flight simulator. Apart from the cost of acquiring one or more multimillion-dollar simulators and other related expenses, airlines that were required by the FAA AEG to train pilots on a full-flight simulator could also lose revenue that the pilot might otherwise have generated from flying airline passengers during that time. Accordingly, if the FAA AEG required a less rigorous level—such as "Level B"—of differences training for the 737 MAX in the 737 MAX FSB Report, the 737 MAX would be a more attractive option for Boeing's airline customers already flying the 737 NG than switching to an entirely new airplane, such as the new version of Company-1's airplane, as such customers would save significant money in pilot-training costs by transitioning to the 737 MAX.
context: Statement of Facts explaining the financial incentive structure: Level B training would make the 737 MAX more competitive and attractive to customers compared to switching to an entirely new aircraft.

label: Program directive not to create differences
original_label: Program directive not to create differences
quote: For example, in an email to Boeing employees including Boeing Employee-2 discussing a potential change to another part of the 737 MAX's flight controls on or about November 10, 2016, Boeing Employee-1 emphasized that "[o]ne of the Program Directives we were given was to not create any differences [. . .]. This is what we sold to the regulators who have already granted us the Level B differences determination. To go back to them now, and tell them there is in fact a difference [. . .] would be a huge threat to that differences training determination."
context: Email from Boeing Employee-1 to subordinates showing how pressure to maintain Level B training was transmitted down and framed as a non-negotiable program directive.

label: Discovered MCAS expanded scope and withheld from FAA
original_label: Discovered MCAS expanded scope and withheld from FAA
quote: On or about November 15, 2016, during a test flight of the 737 MAX in a simulator, Boeing Employee-1 experienced what Boeing Employee-1 recognized as MCAS operating at lower speed. Boeing Employee-1 further recognized that this lower-speed operation was different from what Boeing had briefed and described to the FAA AEG. On or about that same day, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 discussed MCAS in an internal Boeing electronic chat communication, writing in part: Boeing Employee-1: Oh shocker alerT! [sic] / MCAS is now active down to [Mach] .2 / It's running rampant in the sim on me / at least that's what [a Boeing simulator engineer] thinks is happening Boeing Employee-2: Oh great, that means we have to update the speed trim description in vol 2 Boeing Employee-1: so I basically lied to the regulators (unknowingly) Boeing Employee-2: it wasn't a lie, no one told us that was the case
context: Chat communication showing the moment Boeing's chief pilots discovered MCAS's expanded operational scope and recognized it contradicted what they had told the FAA.

label: MCAS expansion created pitch-up problem requiring solution
original_label: MCAS expansion created pitch-up problem requiring solution
quote: To achieve its promised fuel efficiency, the 737 MAX used larger engines than the 737 NG. These larger engines, and their placement under the airplane's wings, meant that the aerodynamics of the 737 MAX differed from those of the 737 NG. These different aerodynamics created a new handling characteristic for the 737 MAX that caused the 737 MAX's nose to pitch up during a certain flight maneuver called a high-speed, wind-up turn. A high-speed, wind-up turn generally involved sharply turning the airplane at high speed (approximately Mach 0.6-0.8) in a corkscrew-like pattern. A high-speed, wind-up turn was a "certification" maneuver, that is, a maneuver outside the limits of what the 737 MAX would be expected to encounter during a normal commercial passenger flight. Nevertheless, if Boeing did not fix the 737 MAX's pitch-up characteristic in high-speed, wind up turns, the FAA could determine that the 737 MAX did not meet U.S. federal airworthiness standards. To fix this pitch-up characteristic, Boeing created MCAS and incorporated it as a part of the 737 MAX's flight controls.
context: Statement of Facts explaining the technical constraint that drove MCAS creation: larger engines created aerodynamic issues that could not be resolved without a solution.

label: Withheld MCAS expansion from FAA AEG deliberately
original_label: Withheld MCAS expansion from FAA AEG deliberately
quote: Despite knowing that the FAA AEG had issued its provisional "Level B" determination without any awareness that MCAS's operational scope had been expanded to include high angle of attack conditions in nearly the entire speed range of ordinary commercial flight, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 did not correct the FAA AEG's understanding of MCAS's operational scope or otherwise ensure that the FAA AEG's "Level B" determination was based on an accurate understanding of MCAS's operation. Instead, Boeing—through Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2—intentionally withheld and concealed from the FAA AEG their knowledge of MCAS's expanded operational scope.
context: Statement of Facts summarizing the deliberate choice not to disclose MCAS expansion to the FAA AEG after discovering it, despite understanding its relevance to the Level B determination.

label: Told FAA to delete MCAS from FSB Report
original_label: Told FAA to delete MCAS from FSB Report
quote: On or about November 22, 2016, the other Boeing employee emailed the draft 737 MAX FSB Report back to the FAA AEG with proposed edits. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 were included on this email. Boeing Employee-1 included a proposed edit to delete a reference to MCAS, and wrote, "We agreed not to reference MCAS since it's outside normal operating envelope." Neither Boeing Employee-1 nor Boeing Employee-2 shared the fact of MCAS's expanded operational scope with the FAA AEG or otherwise corrected the FAA AEG's misimpression that MCAS's operational scope was limited to high-speed, wind-up turns.
context: Email communication showing Boeing's active effort to remove MCAS from the FSB Report while concealing that MCAS's operational scope had been expanded.

label: Reinforced false basis for MCAS deletion from FSB Report
original_label: Reinforced false basis for MCAS deletion from FSB Report
quote: In doing so, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 deceived the FAA AEG into believing that the basis upon which the FAA AEG had initially "agreed" to remove any information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report—that MCAS could only activate during the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind-up turn—remained the same. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 withheld their knowledge of MCAS from the FAA AEG to avoid risking the FAA AEG taking any action that could threaten the differences-training determination for the 737 MAX.
context: Statement of Facts explaining Boeing's motivation to conceal MCAS expansion: fear that disclosure would threaten the Level B training determination.

label: Reiterated MCAS deletion from FSB Report January 2017
original_label: Reiterated MCAS deletion from FSB Report January 2017
quote: On or about January 17, 2017, Boeing Employee-1 again reminded the FAA AEG in an email to delete any reference to MCAS from the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report, and wrote, "Flight Controls: Delete MCAS, recall we decided we weren't going to cover it [. . .] since it's way outside the normal operating envelope." Again, Boeing Employee-1 deceived the FAA AEG into believing that the basis upon which the FAA AEG had initially "decided" to remove any information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report—that MCAS could only activate during the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind-up turn—remained the same.
context: Later email showing Boeing sustained the deception about MCAS by repeatedly telling the FAA that MCAS was outside normal operating envelope.

label: Provisional Level B training approval achieved August 2016
original_label: Provisional Level B training approval achieved August 2016
quote: On or about August 16, 2016, before the FAA AEG published the 737 MAX FSB Report, the FAA AEG issued a provisional "Level B" differences-training determination for the 737 MAX. At the time of this provisional determination, the FAA AEG was unaware that Boeing had expanded MCAS's operational scope. On or about the same day, Boeing Employee-1 recognized Boeing's achievement in an email to Boeing employees, including Boeing Employee-2, and wrote that the FAA AEG's provisional determination "culminates more than 3 years of tireless and collaborative efforts across many business units" and that the 737 MAX program management "is VERY happy."
context: Email communication showing how Boeing leadership celebrated achieving the Level B training goal and the company's satisfaction with this outcome.

label: Fuel efficiency cost savings motivation for Level B
original_label: Fuel efficiency cost savings motivation for Level B
quote: For example, in or around November 2014, Boeing Employee-2 wrote in an internal Boeing electronic chat communication to Boeing Employee-1 that "nothing can jepordize [sic] level b[.]" In or around December 2014, Boeing Employee-1 wrote in an email to another Boeing employee that "if we lose Level B [it] will be thrown squarely on my shoulders. It was [Boeing Employee-1], yes [Boeing Employee-1]! Who cost Boeing tens of millions of dollars!"
context: Chat and email communications showing the financial stakes attached to the Level B determination and how it was framed as a tens-of-millions-of-dollars issue.

label: Knowledge that Level B determination required accurate information
original_label: Knowledge that Level B determination required accurate information
quote: Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 understood that the FAA AEG relied on them, as members of Boeing's 737 MAX Flight Technical Team, to identify and provide to the FAA AEG all information that was relevant to the FAA AEG in connection with the FAA AEG's publication of the 737 MAX FSB Report, including information that could impact the FAA AEG's differences-training determination. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 also understood that, because flight controls were vital to flying modern commercial airplanes, differences between the flight controls of the 737 NG and the 737 MAX were especially important to the FAA AEG for purposes of its publication of the 737 MAX FSB Report and the FAA AEG's differences-training determination.
context: Statement of Facts establishing that Boeing's chief pilots understood their responsibility to provide relevant information about flight control changes to the FAA.

label: Provisional approval assumed no significant system changes
original_label: Provisional approval assumed no significant system changes

label: Production movement prioritized over quality reduction
original_label: Production movement prioritized over quality reduction

label: Software circumvents emissions standards
original_label: Software circumvents emissions standards
quote: On September 18, 2015, the EPA sent a Notice of Violation (NOV) of the Clean Air Act to Volkswagen (Volkswagen AG, Audi AG, and Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.) alleging that four-cylinder Volkswagen and Audi diesel cars sold in the U.S. from model years 2009 to 2015 include software that circumvents EPA emissions standards. label: Defeat device results in excess emissions
original_label: Defeat device results in excess emissions
quote: Known as a "defeat device," this design feature results in the cars emitting up to 40 times the emissions that are allowed to ensure public health is protected. label: VW violated certificate of conformity by concealing defeat device
original_label: VW violated certificate of conformity by concealing defeat device

By making and selling vehicles with defeat devices that allowed for higher levels of air emissions than were certified to the EPA, VW violated multiple important Clean Air Act provisions. These violations are very serious. Not only because the illegal defeat device results in excess emissions many times the allowable standard, but also because after the high emissions were discovered, VW concealed the facts from the EPA, the State of California, and from consumers.

label: Market domination through perceived safety claim
original_label: Market domination through perceived safety claim

original_label: Aggressive marketing to capture emerging pain management market

label: Sales training to promote false safety claims despite internal knowledge
original_label: Sales training to promote false safety claims despite internal knowledge

original_label: False addiction-risk claims to health care providers

label: False training on euphoria and abuse potential
original_label: False training on euphoria and abuse potential

label: False claims about withdrawal and tolerance at lower doses
original_label: False claims about withdrawal and tolerance at lower doses

label: Reinterpreting package insert to claim no euphoria and addiction risk reduction
original_label: Reinterpreting package insert to claim no euphoria and addiction risk reduction

label: Prescription volume growth from aggressive marketing campaign
original_label: Prescription volume growth from aggressive marketing campaign

original_label: Physicians' safety concerns required misrepresentation to overcome

quote: Schon zu Beginn des Untersuchungszeitraums war bekannt, dass dieser Fahrzyklus, der seine heutige Gestalt in den 1990er Jahren erhalten hatte, das reale emissionsrelevante Fahrverhalten nur noch zum Teil widerspiegelt. Kontrollverfahren die Grenzwerte einhalten, diese im realen Fahrbetrieb auf der Straße regelmäßig überschreiten.

context: The investigative report describes the well-known inadequacy of the test procedure used to verify emissions compliance, explaining the gap between laboratory and real-world emissions.

label: Euro 6 diesel cannot meet real-world emissions standards
original_label: Euro 6 diesel cannot meet real-world emissions standards
quote: Laut den Erwägungsgründen der beiden RDE-Verordnungen war Auslöser für die Einführung von RDE-Tests die Beobachtung, dass insbesondere die Stickoxidemissionen von Diesel-Pkw und leichten Nutzfahrzeugen in der Betriebspraxis erheblich über den im NEFZ gemessenen Emissionen liegen und die Grenzwertverschärfungen hier in der Praxis nicht zu der erhofften Emissionsreduzierung führten.

original_label: NEFZ test cycle inadequate for measuring real emissions

original_label: VW pursuing U.S. diesel market entry amid competition

original_label: At normal temperatures outside test window, AGR reduction is technically necessary
quote: Zur Frage der Abschaltung der Abgasrückführung hat der Sachverständige dargelegt, dass bei Hochlast zu viel Ruß entstehe, wenn man nicht ausreichend Zylindervolumen habe. label: Manufacturers required to meet strict Euro 5/6 NOx and CO2 targets simultaneously
original_label: Manufacturers required to meet strict Euro 5/6 NOx and CO2 targets simultaneously
quote: Bei Einführung von Euro-5-Gesetzgebung sei die AGR erstmals auch auf der Niedrigdruckseite verwendet worden. Dieser Begriff umfasse durchaus sog. innermotorische Maßnahmen und beschränke sich nicht auf sog. nachgelagerte Maßnahmen der Abgasreinigung. label: Real-world NOx emissions far exceed laboratory type-approval values
original_label: Real-world NOx emissions far exceed laboratory type-approval values

label: Test procedure constrains how manufacturers can optimize engines
original_label: Test procedure constrains how manufacturers can optimize engines
quote: Es seien auch nicht überprüft worden, ob gezielte Manipulationen bzw. Abschalteinrichtungen dargelegt. label: German automakers competing to meet strict targets with existing technology
original_label: German automakers competing to meet strict targets with existing technology

original_label: Stringent CO2 and NOx reduction mandates from EU successive Euro standards

label: Real NOx emissions from diesel cars remain far above standards despite tighter rules
