However, Enron structured the transaction so that $11.36 million of the supposed outside equity was actually borrowed from Barclays by various entities set up and controlled by Kopper. The Barclays loans were secured by approximately $6.58 million in cash that was generated by JEDI's November 1997 sale of an asset. Those funds were held in accounts that were fully pledged to Barclays, meaning that Barclays was partly protected against risk of loss.
context: SEC complaint showing Enron structured Chewco with largely borrowed funds disguised as equity to manipulate the three-percent independent equity requirement.

label: Oral buyback guarantee instead of written to avoid auditor objection
original_label: Oral buyback guarantee instead of written to avoid auditor objection
quote: Because such a buyback agreement would have destroyed the favorable accounting treatment, the buyback agreement, originally in writing, was not set forth in the final deal documents, but continued in fact as part of an oral understanding. The buyback agreement was also not included in the written documents out of concern that Enron's auditors, Arthur Andersen LLP, would not approve the sale to LJM1 with such a provision.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow deliberately converted a written buyback guarantee into an oral one to conceal it from auditors.

label: Backdated AVICI hedge to lock in inflated gains
original_label: Backdated AVICI hedge to lock in inflated gains
quote: Fastow caused the AVICI hedge to be backdated to August 3, 2000. Fastow chose this date because he knew it was the date AVICI traded at an all time high price of $163.50. By back-dating the AVICI hedge in this manner, Fastow and Enron fraudulently locked in the recognition of a substantial gain and booked $75 million in additional mark to market gains that they otherwise would not have recognized.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow deliberately backdated documents to manipulate the timing of earnings recognition to meet financial targets.

label: Manufactured $41 million payment to disguise side deal
original_label: Manufactured $41 million payment to disguise side deal
quote: To conceal the side deal, Fastow and others devised a scheme to manufacture a $41 million payment to LJM2. Fastow and others made it appear that the payment represented the premium paid on a "put option" on Enron shares that Enron purchased from Talon. Enron purchased the put option, set to expire on October 18, 2000, for a premium of $41 million. Enron settled the put option early and Talon then distributed the $41 million to LJM2. The transaction was unusual for several reasons, including the fact that the put option was a bet by Enron that its own stock price would decline. There was no true business purpose for the put option other than to generate funds to pay LJM2 under the undisclosed side deal.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow deliberately created a sham transaction with no legitimate business purpose to transfer money while concealing the true arrangement.

label: Pressured Financial Institution to invest with fraudulent guarantee
original_label: Pressured Financial Institution to invest with fraudulent guarantee
quote: In spite of some dissension within the Financial Institution, including an internal document expressing concern that it could be viewed as aiding and abetting Enron's fraudulent manipulation of its income statement, the Financial Institution ultimately agreed to invest in the project. The Financial Institution invested $7 million, and Enron financed the remainder of the deal with a $21 million loan that was non-recourse to the Financial Institution. The Financial Institution never paid any interest on the loan. The Financial Institution had no real interest in investing in barge power projects in Nigeria but wanted to accommodate Enron, an important client and source of millions in fees to the Financial Institution. To induce the Financial Institution to enter into the transaction, Fastow guaranteed the Financial Institution that it would not lose money and would be taken out of the deal within six months.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow deliberately pressured an external party into a fraudulent transaction by providing a guarantee that made the risk disappear.

label: Global Galactic agreement to guarantee LJM entities profitability
original_label: Global Galactic agreement to guarantee LJM entities profitability
quote: However, Fastow and the CAO had an undisclosed agreement which was referred to as the "Global Galactical" agreement or "Global Galactic" agreement. Under the agreement, any Enron transaction with the LJM entities that resulted in a loss to the LJM entities would be made up later in subsequent LJM deals. As a result, the LJM entities would not lose money in their dealings with Enron.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow established a covert arrangement to eliminate risk for the supposedly independent LJM entities.

label: Side agreements to guarantee LJM2 did not bear true economic risk
original_label: Side agreements to guarantee LJM2 did not bear true economic risk
quote: Fastow and Enron representatives regularly entered into secret side agreements pursuant to which the LJM entities would not bear true economic risk when they "purchased" assets from Enron. Frequently there was an understanding with Enron that the LJM entities would hold assets only for a short period of time, and Enron guaranteed that the LJM entities would make a profit on the buyback of those assets by Enron.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow systematically eliminated economic risk from LJM deals through secret arrangements contradicting the public structure.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Fastow profited from inflated Enron results and stock
original_label: Fastow profited from inflated Enron results and stock
quote: Fastow's illegal gains from the fraud alleged herein include kickbacks and undisclosed fees. In addition, Fastow made millions in salary, bonuses, and through sales of Enron stock even as he was defrauding Enron, its investors, and others.
context: SEC complaint establishing that Fastow's compensation and stock gains were tied to the financial results he manipulated.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: LJM entities provided personal financial benefit to Fastow
original_label: LJM entities provided personal financial benefit to Fastow
quote: Fastow and the LJM entities engaged in these transactions because: (1) as CFO, Fastow readily could rid Enron of poorly performing assets and thereby improve Enron's reported financial results, which in turn would enable Fastow to earn continued prestige, salary, bonuses, and other benefits from Enron; (2) the LJM entities would make money on their dealings with Enron, since Enron illegally and secretly guaranteed that the LJM entities would not lose money and, if they did, would be made whole in future transactions; and (3) Fastow and others at the LJM entities personally reaped huge sums of money from such transactions, both in the form of management fees and skimmed deal profits.
context: SEC complaint explaining the personal financial incentives driving Fastow's fraudulent transactions, including compensation tied to reported results.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Kopper received management fees and purchase option proceeds
original_label: Kopper received management fees and purchase option proceeds
quote: From December 1997 through December 2000, Fastow directed Kopper to secretly share with him various payments received by Kopper relating to Chewco. Kopper received a total of approximately $1.5 million in "management fees" relating to Chewco, which he shared with Fastow at his direction mainly through checks payable to members of Fastow's family. Fastow directed Kopper to pay at least $54,000 to Fastow's wife for administrative work she did for Chewco. In December 1998, Fastow caused Enron to pay a $400,000 "nuisance fee" to Chewco as compensation for agreeing to amend JEDI's partnership agreement, even though the amendment benefitted Chewco, not Enron. At Fastow's direction, Kopper transferred approximately $67,224 of the nuisance fee back to Fastow, again through checks written to Fastow or members of his family.
context: SEC complaint detailing the various forms of personal compensation that Fastow derived from fraudulent transactions.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Southampton transaction distributed millions to insiders
original_label: Southampton transaction distributed millions to insiders
quote: As a result, the three NatWest bankers who participated in the scheme received approximately $7.3 million. The balance of the funds went to Fastow, Kopper and other investors in an entity called Southampton Place LP ("Southampton"), which Kopper created. The Southampton "investors" were a purported charitable foundation set up by Fastow for the purpose of receiving Southampton proceeds, which contributed $25,000 and received approximately $4.5 million; Kopper, who contributed $25,000 and caused Chewco to loan another $680,000, and received approximately $4.5 million; and five Enron and LJM employees chosen by Kopper and Fastow, who contributed a total of less than $20,000 and received a total of approximately $3.3 million.
context: SEC complaint showing how insiders received disproportionate returns on minimal capital investments through the Southampton scheme.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: RADR windfall demanded and distributed to Fastow
original_label: RADR windfall demanded and distributed to Fastow
quote: RADR proved to be far more lucrative than initially expected, generating a "windfall" to the investors. Fastow became aware of the windfall and demanded a share, in the form of kickbacks through Kopper of investors' RADR proceeds. In all, records reflect that Kopper arranged "gift" payments totaling approximately $125,000 to Fastow and his family between December 1997 and February 2000.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow actively seized opportunities to personally capture profits from successful fraudulent deals.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Kopper purchased general partner interests for millions
original_label: Kopper purchased general partner interests for millions
quote: Kopper purchased the general partner interest in the entity and another entity from Fastow for approximately $16.5 million. On August 21, 2002, Kopper pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering and agreed to forfeit $4 million in criminal proceeds.
context: SEC complaint documenting Kopper's substantial financial gains from his role in the fraudulent LJM entities.

label: Fastow controlled and directed Kopper's actions and distributions
original_label: Fastow controlled and directed Kopper's actions and distributions
quote: At all times relevant, Fastow, directly and indirectly, was a control person of Enron and Michael J. Kopper within the meaning of the federal securities laws. From December 1997 through December 2000, Fastow directed Kopper to secretly share with him various payments received by Kopper relating to Chewco.
context: SEC complaint showing Fastow used his authority to direct subordinate Kopper to execute fraudulent transactions and distribute proceeds.

label: Enron raising billions while achieving growth targets
original_label: Enron raising billions while achieving growth targets
quote: From 1997 to 2001, while Fastow engaged in the fraudulent conduct alleged herein, Enron raised approximately $5 billion in the public debt and equity markets. Among other operations, Enron was the nation's largest natural gas and electric marketer with reported annual revenue of more than $150 billion. Enron rose to number seven on the Fortune 500 list of companies. By December 2, 2001, when it filed for bankruptcy, Enron's stock price had dropped in less than a year from more than $80 per share to less than $1.
context: SEC complaint providing context on Enron's scale, ambitions, and capital market pressures to sustain aggressive growth and financial targets.

label: Rapid sales growth and market dominance objective
original_label: Rapid sales growth and market dominance objective
quote: Sales of the drug increased rapidly following its introduction to the marketplace in 1996. By 2001, sales had exceeded $1 billion annually, and OxyContin had become the most frequently prescribed brand-name narcotic medication for treating moderate-to-severe pain in the United States.
context: GAO report documenting Purdue's rapid expansion of OxyContin sales into market leadership position.

label: Expand prescribing base beyond cancer pain to primary care
original_label: Expand prescribing base beyond cancer pain to primary care
quote: From the outset of the OxyContin marketing campaign, Purdue promoted the drug to physicians for noncancer pain conditions that can be caused by arthritis, injuries, and chronic diseases, in addition to cancer pain. Purdue directed its sales representatives to focus on the physicians in their sales territories who were high opioid prescribers. This group included cancer and pain specialists, primary care physicians, and physicians who were high prescribers of Purdue's older product, MS Contin. One of Purdue's goals was to identify primary care physicians who would expand the company's OxyContin prescribing base.
context: GAO analysis of Purdue's documented marketing strategy showing explicit objective to shift OxyContin from cancer to noncancer pain and recruit primary care physicians.

label: Primary care physicians as half of prescriber base
original_label: Primary care physicians as half of prescriber base
quote: Purdue has stated that by 2003 primary care physicians had grown to constitute nearly half of all OxyContin prescribers, based on data from IMS Health, an information service providing pharmaceutical market research.
context: GAO report noting Purdue's achievement of goal to establish primary care physicians as major prescriber segment.

label: OxyContin as competitive response to other opioids
original_label: OxyContin as competitive response to other opioids
quote: Fortuitous timing may have contributed to this growth, as the launching of the drug occurred during the national focus on the inadequacy of patient pain treatment and management. In 1997, OxyContin's sales and prescriptions began increasing significantly, and they continued to increase through 2002.
context: GAO explaining how Purdue capitalized on market conditions and movement to treat pain more aggressively.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Sales representative bonuses tied to OxyContin sales growth
original_label: Sales representative bonuses tied to OxyContin sales growth
quote: Purdue stated it offered a better than industry average salary and sales bonuses to attract top sales representatives and provide incentives to boost OxyContin sales as it had done for MS Contin. Although the sales representatives were primarily focused on OxyContin promotion, the amount of the bonus depended on whether a representative met the sales quotas in his or her sales territory for all company products. As OxyContin's sales increased, Purdue's growth-based portion of the bonus formula increased the OxyContin sales quotas necessary to earn the same base sales bonus amounts.
context: GAO detailing Purdue's compensation structure that created escalating targets and performance pressure on sales representatives.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Bonus escalation from $1 million to $40 million
original_label: Bonus escalation from $1 million to $40 million
quote: The amount of total bonuses that Purdue estimated were tied to OxyContin sales increased significantly from about $1 million in 1996, when OxyContin was first marketed, to about $40 million in 2001. Beginning in 2000, when the newly created hospital specialty representatives began promoting OxyContin, their estimated total bonuses were approximately $6 million annually. In 2001, the average annual salary for a Purdue sales representative was $55,000, and the average annual bonus was $71,500. During the same year, the highest annual sales bonus was nearly $240,000, and the lowest was nearly $15,000.
context: GAO quantifying the magnitude of bonus structure tied to OxyContin sales, showing dramatic escalation of financial incentives.

category: Incentives and rewards tied to targets
label: Single physician bonus practice before 2001
original_label: Single physician bonus practice before 2001
quote: In 2001, Purdue decided to limit the sales bonus a representative could earn based on the growth in prescribing of a single physician after a meeting with the U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Virginia at which the company was informed of the possibility that a bonus could be based on the prescribing of one physician.
context: GAO reporting that Purdue modified bonus structure only after federal prosecutor warned about practice of tying bonuses to individual high-prescribing physicians.

label: Sales representatives expected to make 35 calls per week
original_label: Sales representatives expected to make 35 calls per week
quote: Each Purdue sales representative has a specific sales territory and is responsible for developing a list of about 105 to 140 physicians to call on who already prescribe opioids or who are candidates for prescribing opioids. In 1996, the 300-plus Purdue sales representatives had a total physician call list of approximately 33,400 to 44,500. By 2000, the nearly 700 representatives had a total call list of approximately 70,500 to 94,000 physicians. Each Purdue sales representative is expected to make about 35 physician calls per week and typically calls on each physician every 3 to 4 weeks.
context: GAO documenting the volume and frequency demands placed on Purdue sales representatives to drive physician engagement.

label: Promotional messages downplaying OxyContin risks
original_label: Promotional messages downplaying OxyContin risks
quote: From OxyContin's launch until its July 2001 label change, Purdue used two key promotional messages for primary care physicians and other high prescribers. The first was that physicians should prescribe OxyContin for their pain patients both as the drug to start with and to stay with. The second contrasted dosing with other opioid pain relievers with OxyContin dosing as the hard way versus the easy way to dose because OxyContin's twice-a-day dosing was more convenient for patients.
context: GAO documenting Purdue's core promotional messages that emphasized convenience and broad use while downplaying or omitting risk information.

label: Promotional video claiming low addiction rate without substantiation
original_label: Promotional video claiming low addiction rate without substantiation
quote: The video included a statement that opioid analgesics have been shown to cause addiction in less than 1 percent of patients. According to FDA, this statement has not been substantiated.
context: GAO reporting that Purdue distributed promotional video with unsubstantiated addiction claim to allay physician concerns about risk.

label: Video distributed without FDA review for three years
original_label: Video distributed without FDA review for three years
quote: Beginning in 1998, Purdue, as part of its marketing and promotion of OxyContin, distributed 15,000 copies of an OxyContin video to physicians without submitting it to FDA for review. This video, entitled I Got My Life Back: Patients in Pain Tell Their Story, presented the pain relief experiences of various patients and the pain medications, including OxyContin, they had been prescribed. FDA regulations require pharmaceutical manufacturers to submit all promotional materials for approved prescription drug products to the agency at the time of their initial use. Because Purdue did not comply with this regulation, FDA did not have an opportunity to review the video to ensure that the information it contained was truthful, balanced, and accurately communicated. Purdue has acknowledged the oversight of not submitting the video to FDA for review.
context: GAO documenting Purdue's deliberate or negligent failure to submit promotional video for FDA review, allowing three years of unsupervised distribution.

label: FDA found second video minimized risks and made unsubstantiated claims
original_label: FDA found second video minimized risks and made unsubstantiated claims
quote: In February 2001, Purdue submitted a second version of the video to FDA, which included information about the 160-milligram OxyContin tablet. FDA did not review this second version until October 2002, after we inquired about its content. FDA told us it found that the second version of the video appeared to make unsubstantiated claims regarding OxyContin's effect on patients' quality of life and ability to perform daily activities and minimized the risks associated with the drug.
context: GAO report of FDA's post-hoc review finding that Purdue's second video contained unsubstantiated efficacy claims and risk minimization.

label: FDA cited twice for misleading advertisements
original_label: FDA cited twice for misleading advertisements
quote: Purdue has been cited twice by FDA for using advertisements in professional medical journals that violated the FD&C Act. In May 2000, FDA issued an untitled letter to Purdue regarding a professional medical journal advertisement for OxyContin. FDA noted that among other problems, the advertisement implied that OxyContin had been studied for all types of arthritis pain when it had been studied only in patients with moderate-to-severe osteoarthritis pain, the advertisement suggested OxyContin could be used as an initial therapy for the treatment of osteoarthritis pain without substantial evidence to support this claim, and the advertisement promoted OxyContin in a selected class of patients—the elderly—without presenting risk information applicable to that class of patients.
context: GAO documenting FDA enforcement action against Purdue for multiple violations in medical journal advertisements.

label: Warning letter for minimizing risks and overstating efficacy
original_label: Warning letter for minimizing risks and overstating efficacy
quote: The second action taken by FDA was more serious. In January 2003, FDA issued a warning letter to Purdue regarding two professional medical journal advertisements for OxyContin that minimized its risks and overstated its efficacy, by failing to prominently present information from the boxed warning on the potentially fatal risks associated with OxyContin and its abuse liability, along with omitting important information about the limitations on the indicated use of OxyContin.
context: GAO documenting more serious FDA enforcement action for advertisements that systematically minimized fatal risks and abuse liability.

label: Original label inadvertently provided method to abuse drug
original_label: Original label inadvertently provided method to abuse drug
quote: The safety warning on the OxyContin label may also have contributed to the drug's potential for abuse and diversion, by inadvertently providing abusers with information on how the drug could be misused. The label included the warning that the tablets should not be broken, chewed, or crushed because such action could result in the rapid release and absorption of a potentially toxic dose of oxycodone. FDA places similar safety warnings on other drugs to ensure that they are used properly. FDA officials stated that neither they nor other experts anticipated that crushing the controlled-release tablet and intravenously injecting or snorting the drug would become widespread and lead to a high level of abuse.
context: GAO explaining how the original FDA-approved warning label, intended as a safety measure, inadvertently communicated abuse methods to potential misusers.

label: Doubled sales force to expand prescriber base
original_label: Doubled sales force to expand prescriber base
quote: Purdue significantly increased its sales force to market and promote OxyContin to physicians and other health care practitioners. In 1996, Purdue began promoting OxyContin with a sales force of approximately 300 representatives in its Prescription Sales Division. Through a 1996 copromotion agreement, Abbott Laboratories provided at least another 300 representatives, doubling the total OxyContin sales force. By 2000, Purdue had more than doubled its own internal sales force to 671.
context: GAO documenting Purdue's strategic expansion of sales force as part of aggressive marketing objective.

label: Promotional conference circuit at resort locations
original_label: Promotional conference circuit at resort locations
quote: During the first 5 years that OxyContin was marketed, Purdue conducted over 40 national pain management and speaker training conferences, usually in resort locations such as Boca Raton, Florida, and Scottsdale, Arizona, to recruit and train health care practitioners for its national speaker bureau. The trained speakers were then made available to speak about the appropriate use of opioids, including oxycodone, the active ingredient in OxyContin, to their colleagues in various settings, such as local medical conferences and grand round presentations in hospitals involving physicians, residents, and interns. Over the 5 years, these conferences were attended by more than 5,000 physicians, pharmacists, and nurses, whose travel, lodging, and meal costs were paid by the company.
context: GAO documenting Purdue's extensive investment in speaker training conferences at upscale venues to recruit physician advocates.

label: OxyContin spending 6-12 times higher than competitors
original_label: OxyContin spending 6-12 times higher than competitors
quote: According to DEA's analysis of IMS Health data, Purdue spent approximately 6 to 12 times more on promotional efforts during OxyContin's first 6 years on the market than it had spent on its older product, MS Contin, during its first 6 years, or than had been spent by Janssen Pharmaceutical Products, L.P., for one of OxyContin's drug competitors, Duragesic.
context: GAO comparing Purdue's promotional spending to competitors and its own earlier product, showing significantly aggressive investment.

label: Branded promotional items unprecedented for schedule II opioids
original_label: Branded promotional items unprecedented for schedule II opioids
quote: As part of its marketing campaign, Purdue distributed several types of branded promotional items to health care practitioners. Among these items were OxyContin fishing hats, stuffed plush toys, coffee mugs with heat-activated messages, music compact discs, luggage tags, and pens containing a pullout conversion chart showing physicians how to calculate the dosage to convert a patient to OxyContin from other opioid pain relievers. In May 2002, in anticipation of PhRMA's voluntary guidance for sales representatives' interactions with health care professionals, Purdue instructed its sales force to destroy any remaining inventory of non-health-related promotional items, such as stuffed toys or golf balls. In early 2003, Purdue began distributing an OxyContin branded goniometer—a range and motion measurement guide. According to DEA, Purdue's use of branded promotional items to market OxyContin was unprecedented among schedule II opioids, and was an indicator of Purdue's aggressive and inappropriate marketing of OxyContin.
context: GAO and DEA characterizing Purdue's consumer-style branded merchandise as unprecedented violation of industry norms for controlled substances.

label: Patient coupon program for free initial prescriptions
original_label: Patient coupon program for free initial prescriptions
quote: For the first time in marketing any of its products, Purdue used a patient starter coupon program for OxyContin to provide patients with a free limited-time prescription. Unlike patient assistance programs, which provide free prescriptions to patients in financial need, a coupon program is intended to enable a patient to try a new drug through a one-time free prescription. A sales representative distributes coupons to a physician, who decides whether to offer one to a patient, and then the patient redeems it for a free prescription through a participating pharmacy. The program began in 1998 and ran intermittently for 4 years. In 1998 and 1999, each sales representative had 25 coupons that were redeemable for a free 30-day supply. In 2000 each representative had 90 coupons for a 7-day supply, and in 2001 each had 10 coupons for a 7-day supply. Approximately 34,000 coupons had been redeemed nationally when the program was terminated following the July 2001 OxyContin label change.
context: GAO documenting Purdue's novel use of free prescription coupons to build patient demand for new controlled substance.

label: Medical education funding to facilitate hospital access
original_label: Medical education funding to facilitate hospital access
quote: From 1996, when OxyContin was introduced to the market, to July 2002, Purdue has funded over 20,000 pain-related educational programs through direct sponsorship or financial grants. These grants included support for programs to provide physicians with opportunities to earn required continuing medical education credits, such as grand round presentations at hospitals and medical education seminars at state and local medical conferences. During 2001 and 2002, Purdue funded a series of nine programs throughout the country to educate hospital physicians and staff on how to comply with JCAHO's pain standards for hospitals and to discuss postoperative pain treatment. Purdue was one of only two drug companies that provided funding for JCAHO's pain management educational programs. Under an agreement with JCAHO, Purdue was the only drug company allowed to distribute certain educational videos and a book about pain management; these materials were also available for purchase from JCAHO's Web site. Purdue's participation in these activities with JCAHO may have facilitated its access to hospitals to promote OxyContin.
context: GAO analyzing Purdue's strategic use of medical education funding and JCAHO partnership to gain exclusive access to hospital prescribers.

label: FDA did not anticipate injectable abuse method
original_label: FDA did not anticipate injectable abuse method
quote: When OxyContin was approved, FDA did not recognize that if the drug is dissolved in water and injected its controlled-release characteristics could be disrupted, creating an immediate rush or high and thereby increasing the potential for misuse and abuse. DEA officials told us that OxyContin became a target for abusers and diverters because the tablet contained larger amounts of active ingredient and the controlled-release formulation was easy for abusers to compromise.
context: GAO explaining that FDA's original assumption about the abuse-resistant properties of controlled-release formulation proved incorrect.

label: Original label claimed low abuse potential
original_label: Original label claimed low abuse potential
quote: OxyContin's controlled-release formulation, which delayed the drug's absorption, also led FDA to include language in the original label stating that OxyContin had a lower potential for abuse than other oxycodone products. FDA officials thought that the controlled-release feature would make the drug less attractive to abusers. However, FDA did not recognize that the drug could be dissolved in water and injected, which disrupted the controlled-release characteristics and created an immediate rush or high, thereby increasing the potential for abuse.
context: GAO explaining how FDA's original label claims about low abuse potential became a liability once abuse patterns emerged.

label: Failure to promote according to label results in discipline
original_label: Failure to promote according to label results in discipline
quote: Purdue reiterated to its sales representatives that failure to promote products according to the approved label, promotional materials, and applicable FDA standards would result in disciplinary action by the company.
context: GAO reporting threat of disciplinary action communicated to sales representatives for deviations from approved messaging.

label: Noncancer pain prescriptions grew tenfold faster than cancer pain
original_label: Noncancer pain prescriptions grew tenfold faster than cancer pain
quote: Purdue's promotion of OxyContin for the treatment of noncancer pain contributed to a greater increase in prescriptions for noncancer pain than for cancer pain from 1997 through 2002. According to IMS Health data, the annual number of OxyContin prescriptions for noncancer pain increased nearly tenfold, from about 670,000 in 1997 to about 6.2 million in 2002. In contrast, during the same 6 years, the annual number of OxyContin prescriptions for cancer pain increased about fourfold, from about 250,000 in 1997 to just over 1 million in 2002.
context: GAO documenting the shift in market composition showing noncancer pain prescriptions becoming 85% of the market as a result of Purdue's promotion strategy.

label: DEA concern about promotion to untrained physicians
original_label: DEA concern about promotion to untrained physicians
quote: DEA has expressed concern that Purdue's aggressive marketing of OxyContin focused on promoting the drug to treat a wide range of conditions to physicians who may not have been adequately trained in pain management. Purdue's sales representatives promoted OxyContin to physicians as an initial opioid treatment for moderate-to-severe pain lasting more than a few days, to be prescribed instead of other single-entity opioid analgesics or short-acting combination opioid pain relievers.
context: GAO quoting DEA's official position that Purdue promoted OxyContin to insufficiently trained physicians across broad indications.

label: Purdue delayed use of prescribing data to identify abuse patterns
original_label: Purdue delayed use of prescribing data to identify abuse patterns
quote: Although Purdue has used very specific information on physician prescribing practices to market and promote OxyContin since its approval, it was not until October 2002 that Purdue began to use this information and other indicators to identify patterns of prescribing that could point to possible improper sales representative promotion or physician abuse and diversion of OxyContin.
context: GAO documenting that Purdue had prescribing data available for marketing purposes but delayed using it for abuse detection.

label: Medical journal advertising spending increased to $4.6 million
original_label: Medical journal advertising spending increased to $4.6 million
quote: Another approach Purdue used to promote OxyContin was to place advertisements in medical journals. Purdue's annual spending for OxyContin advertisements increased from about $700,000 in 1996 to about $4.6 million in 2001.
context: GAO tracking escalation of Purdue's medical journal advertising budget over first six years of OxyContin marketing.

label: Promoted OxyContin for unapproved postoperative use
original_label: Promoted OxyContin for unapproved postoperative use
quote: In addition, in follow-up discussions with Purdue officials on the January 2003 warning letter, FDA expressed concerns about some of the information on Purdue's Partners Against Pain Web site. The Web site appeared to suggest unapproved uses of OxyContin for postoperative pain that may have been inconsistent with OxyContin's labeling and lacked risk information about the drug. For example, one section of the Web site did not disclose that OxyContin is not indicated for pain in the immediate postoperative period—the first 12 to 24 hours following surgery—for patients not previously taking the drug, because its safety in this setting has not been established.
context: GAO documenting FDA's finding that Purdue's web content promoted OxyContin for unapproved postoperative uses without required risk disclosures.

label: Annual sales target exceeded $1 billion by 2001
original_label: Annual sales target exceeded $1 billion by 2001
quote: By 2001, sales had exceeded $1 billion annually, and OxyContin had become the most frequently prescribed brand-name narcotic medication for treating moderate-to-severe pain in the United States.
context: GAO opening statement documenting Purdue's achievement of $1 billion annual sales milestone.

label: OxyContin became main product driving company growth
original_label: OxyContin became main product driving company growth
quote: The drug became Purdue's main product, accounting for 90 percent of the company's total prescription sales by 2001.
context: GAO noting OxyContin's centrality to Purdue's business and revenue generation.

label: US diesel market expansion strategy
original_label: US diesel market expansion strategy
quote: This hearing will examine the available facts and the initial compliance and consumer issues stemming from Volkswagen AG's reported use of engine software that would reduce the effectiveness of emissions control systems in certain make and model year diesel passenger vehicles in the United States, in apparent violation of the Clean Air Act and its implementing regulations.
context: House Committee majority staff memo describing the hearing agenda to examine VW's diesel vehicle strategy in the US market.

label: Diesel vehicles could not meet emissions standards legitimately
original_label: Diesel vehicles could not meet emissions standards legitimately
quote: The agency alleged that VW installed engine software that "sensed" when the vehicles were undergoing emissions testing and ensured emissions control systems were operating to pass the tests. During normal vehicle use, according to the agency, the software would "switch" to a different mode that produced emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) up to 10 to 40 times above current EPA standards.
context: House Committee staff summarizing EPA's allegations that VW's diesel vehicles could only meet emissions tests through deceptive software switching, implying they could not meet standards during normal operation.

label: Installation of defeat device software
original_label: Installation of defeat device software
quote: On September 18, 2015, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued a Notice of Violation (NOV) to Volkswagen AG, Audi AG, and Volkswagen Group of America (collectively, VW) based on a determination "that VW manufactured and installed defeat devices" in certain model year Volkswagen and Audi diesel passenger cars.
context: House Committee staff documenting EPA's formal determination that VW intentionally manufactured and installed defeat devices in diesel vehicles.

label: Defeat device reduces emissions control effectiveness
original_label: Defeat device reduces emissions control effectiveness
quote: The installation and use of a component — in this case engine software — to "bypass, defeat, or render inoperative elements of the vehicles' emission control system," would violate the Clean Air Act (CAA) and EPA regulations. The alleged violations involve MY2009 to MY2015 VW and Audi vehicles equipped with 2.0 liter diesel engines, a vehicle population of approximately 480,000 in the United States.
context: House Committee staff explaining the legal violation and scope of the defeat device installation across 480,000 US vehicles.

label: VW admitted to designing defeat device
original_label: VW admitted to designing defeat device
quote: September 3, 2015: VW admitted to EPA and CARB that it had designed and installed what was effectively a defeat device into these vehicles.
context: House Committee timeline documenting VW's own admission to federal regulators that it had designed and installed the defeat device.

label: 2000-pound car at 2000-dollar price
original_label: 2000-pound car at 2000-dollar price
quote: In 1968, Ford began designing a new subcompact automobile which ultimately became the Pinto. Mr. Iacocca, then a Ford vice president, conceived the project and was its moving force. Ford's objective was to build a car at or below 2,000 pounds to sell for no more than $2,000.
context: Court opinion describing Ford's stated design goal for the Pinto at project inception.

label: Styling dictated engineering to unusual degree
original_label: Styling dictated engineering to unusual degree
quote: Ordinarily marketing surveys and preliminary engineering studies precede the styling of a new automobile line. Pinto, however, was a rush project, so that styling preceded engineering and dictated engineering design to a greater degree than usual. Among the engineering decisions dictated by styling was the placement of the fuel tank.
context: Court opinion explaining how the compressed schedule forced design compromises in the Pinto development.

label: Fuel tank placement constrained by styling
original_label: Fuel tank placement constrained by styling
quote: It was then the preferred practice in Europe and Japan to locate the gas tank over the rear axle in subcompacts because a small vehicle has less 'crush space' between the rear axle and the bumper than larger cars. The Pinto's styling, however, required the tank to be placed behind the rear axle leaving only 9 or 10 inches of 'crush space'--far less than in any other American automobile or Ford overseas subcompact.
context: Court opinion detailing how the Pinto's styling requirements prevented the safer fuel tank location used elsewhere.

label: Crash tests showed defects; fixes available but deferred
original_label: Crash tests showed defects; fixes available but deferred
quote: The crash tests revealed that the Pinto's fuel system as designed could not meet the 20-mile-per-hour proposed standard. Mechanical prototypes struck from the rear with a moving barrier at 21 miles per hour caused the fuel tank to be driven forward and to be punctured, causing fuel leakage in excess of the standard prescribed by the proposed regulation. A production Pinto crash tested at 21 miles per hour into a fixed barrier caused the fuel neck to be torn from the gas tank and the tank to be punctured by a bolt head on the differential housing.
context: Court opinion summarizing crash test results showing the Pinto failed safety standards.

label: Inexpensive fixes available but not implemented
original_label: Inexpensive fixes available but not implemented
quote: The vulnerability of the production Pinto's fuel tank at speeds of 20 and 30-miles-per-hour fixed barrier tests could have been remedied by inexpensive 'fixes,' but Ford produced and sold the Pinto to the public without doing anything to remedy the defects. Design changes that would have enhanced the integrity of the fuel tank system at relatively little cost per car included the following: Longitudinal side members and cross members at $2.40 and $1.80, respectively; a single shock absorbant 'flak suit' to protect the tank at $4; a tank within a tank and placement of the tank over the axle at $5.08 to $5.79; a nylon bladder within the tank at $5.25 to $8; placement of the tank over the axle surrounded with a protective barrier at a cost of $9.95 per car; substitution of a rear axle with a smooth differential housing at a cost of $2.10; imposition of a protective shield between the differential housing and the tank at $2.35; improvement and reenforcement of the bumper at $2.60; addition of eight inches of crush space a cost of $6.40.
context: Court opinion cataloguing specific low-cost design alternatives that Ford rejected.

label: Management knew of defects and crash tests
original_label: Management knew of defects and crash tests
quote: The Pinto crash tests results had been forwarded up the chain of command to the ultimate decision-makers and were known to the Ford officials who decided to go forward with production. Harley Copp, a former Ford engineer and executive in charge of the crash testing program, testified that the highest level of Ford's management made the decision to go forward with the production of the Pinto, knowing that the gas tank was vulnerable to puncture and rupture at low rear impact speeds creating a significant risk of death or injury from fire and knowing that 'fixes' were feasible at nominal cost. He testified that management's decision was based on the cost savings which would inure from omitting or delaying the 'fixes.'
context: Court opinion presenting witness testimony that Ford's top management made the decision to proceed despite known fuel tank defects.

label: Cost-benefit analysis balancing lives against profits
original_label: Cost-benefit analysis balancing lives against profits
quote: At an April 1971 product review meeting chaired by Mr. MacDonald, those present received and discussed a report (exhibit 125) prepared by Ford engineers pertaining to the financial impact of a proposed federal standard on fuel system integrity and the cost savings which would accrue from deferring even minimal 'fixes.' The report refers to crash tests of the integrity of the fuel system of Ford vehicles and design changes needed to meet anticipated federal standards.
context: Court opinion describing a management meeting where Ford engineers presented cost savings from deferring safety fixes.

label: Deferral of fixes to realize savings
original_label: Deferral of fixes to realize savings
quote: A report presented at a Ford production review meeting in April 1971, recommending action to be taken in anticipation of the promulgation of federal standards on fuel system integrity. The report recommended, inter alia, deferral from 1974 to 1976 of the adoption of 'flak suits' or 'bladders' in all Ford cars, including the Pinto, in order to realize a savings of $20.9 million. The report stated that the cost of the flak suit or bladder would be $4 to $8 per car. The meeting at which the report was presented was chaired by Vice President Harold MacDonald and attended by Vice President Robert Alexander and occurred sometime before the 1972 Pinto was placed on the market.
context: Court opinion describing Exhibit 125, a Ford management report quantifying savings from deferring fuel system safety fixes.

label: Engineers complained of unwillingness to deviate for cost
original_label: Engineers complained of unwillingness to deviate for cost
quote: Mr. Copp testified to conversations in late 1968 or early 1969 with the chief assistant research engineer in charge of cost-weight evaluation of the Pinto, and to a later conversation with the chief chassis engineer who was then in charge of crash testing the early prototype. In these conversations, both men expressed concern about the integrity of the Pinto's fuel system and complained about management's unwillingness to deviate from the design if the change would cost money.
context: Court opinion describing testimony from Ford engineers expressing concerns that management would not allow design changes due to cost.

label: Standard required repackaging or major rear structure changes
original_label: Standard required repackaging or major rear structure changes
quote: A September 23, 1970, report (exhibit 124) by Ford's 'Chassis Design Office' concerning a program 'to establish a corporate [Ford] position and reply to the government' on the proposed federal fuel system integrity stand ard which included zero fuel spillage at 20 miles per hour fixed barrier crash by January 1, 1972, and 30 miles per hour by January 1, 1973. The report states in part: 'The 20 and 30 mph rear fixed barrier crashes will probably require repackaging the fuel tanks in a protected area such as above the rear axle. This is based on moving barrier crash tests of a Chevelle and a Ford at 30 mph and other Ford products at 20 mph. Currently there are no plans for forward models to repackage the fuel tanks. Tests must be conducted to prove that repackaged tanks will live without significantly strengthening rear structure for added protection.' The report also notes that the Pinto was the '[smallest] car line with most difficulty in achieving compliance.'
context: Court opinion quoting an internal Ford report showing the engineering challenge posed by federal fuel system integrity standards.

label: EU climate policy incentivizes diesel for CO2 reduction
original_label: EU climate policy incentivizes diesel for CO2 reduction
quote: The increased share of diesel cars in the fleet was also due to the generally lower cost of diesel fuel and the incentives given in the context of EU climate policy to diesel technology as being more fuel-efficient and less CO2-emitting than gasoline
context: The report describes how EU climate objectives created a structural push toward diesel adoption across manufacturers and policy, establishing a key goal of CO2 reduction that conflicted with NOx control.

label: Euro 6 limits unachievable in real use without trade-off
original_label: Euro 6 limits unachievable in real use without trade-off
quote: Evidence shows that the Euro 6 emission limits can be met in real-world conditions regardless of fuel type, if appropriate widely available technology is used. This implies that some car manufacturers have opted to use technology that assures compliance with emission limits only in laboratory test, not for technical reasons but for economic reasons.
context: The committee's findings conclude that manufacturers chose suboptimal emissions control strategies for cost rather than technical inability, indicating legitimate means existed but economic pressure made them unacceptable.

label: Three-year delay to meet Euro 6 standards in real driving
original_label: Three-year delay to meet Euro 6 standards in real driving
quote: Rather than waiting for a new, more realistic and certified test procedure, the co-legislators decided to continue with the development of the Euro 5/6 legislation in 2007, while at the same time giving a mandate to the Commission to keep the test cycles under review, and revise them if necessary to adequately reflect the emissions generated by real driving on the road, included by the legislators in 2007. This resulted in the development and introduction of real driving emission (RDE) testing with portable emission measurement systems (PEMS) into the EU type-approval procedure as of 2017, alongside the introduction of the notion of a conformity factor, which, in practice, weakens the emission standards currently in force.
context: The report describes how legislators chose to maintain weak laboratory-only testing despite knowing it was inadequate, forcing manufacturers to work within inadequate legitimate means for over a decade.

label: VW's aggressive US diesel market entry
original_label: VW's aggressive US diesel market entry
quote: It is justified to propose a lower NOx emission limit for diesel cars since there are standards in the world that are much stricter than those currently in force in the EU and because the technology already exists to reduce NOx emissions since EU car manufacturers are already placing diesel cars on the US market that have to comply with much lower NOx emission limits.
context: The report notes that EU manufacturers including VW were simultaneously selling diesel cars in the stricter US market at 44 mg/km NOx limits while selling the same products in Europe at 80 mg/km, indicating competitive pressure to maintain market share across regions.

label: Diesel market share critical to EU fleet targets
original_label: Diesel market share critical to EU fleet targets
quote: The market share of diesel-powered passenger cars has grown in the European Union over recent decades to a level where these vehicles now represent more than half of new cars sold in almost every Member State; whereas this sustained growth in market share of diesel vehicles also came about as a result of EU climate policy, as diesel technology has an advantage over petrol engines when it comes to CO2 emissions
context: The report establishes that diesel became central to achieving EU fleet CO2 targets, creating a structural dependency that made abandoning diesel technology economically impossible for manufacturers.

label: Euro 6 entry did not improve real-world emissions
original_label: Euro 6 entry did not improve real-world emissions
quote: The introduction of the Euro 6 standards, which were supposed to address, among other things, the issue of NOx emissions, did not improve the situation in the case of most cars. The entry into force of the stricter NOx emission limit of 80 mg/km increased the relative magnitude of the discrepancies between laboratory emissions and real-world emissions, as the latter have stayed essentially constant for the last 15 years
context: The report shows that despite tightening regulatory targets, actual on-road emissions from the vehicle fleet did not improve, creating a gap between compliance appearance and real performance.

label: Industry resistance slowed RDE adoption in working groups
original_label: Industry resistance slowed RDE adoption in working groups
quote: The Commission services were concerned about the car manufacturers' resistance to the introduction of PEMS testing
context: Internal Commission documents reveal that manufacturers exercised pressure in technical working groups to oppose real-world testing methods that would have exposed their emissions strategies.

label: Industry experts overrepresented in RDE working group
original_label: Industry experts overrepresented in RDE working group
quote: Over half of the RDE-LDV working group participants consisted of experts from car manufacturers and other automotive industries. This can inter alia be attributed to the lack of sufficient technical expertise in the Commission departments. While the Commission consulted a wide range of stakeholders and ensured open access to the RDE-LDV group, it should have taken further steps to 'as far as possible, ensure a balanced representation of relevant stakeholders, taking into account the specific tasks of the expert group and the type of expertise required', as required by the horizontal rules for Commission expert groups of 10 November 2010.
context: The inquiry found that manufacturers dominated the technical committees developing emissions testing standards, allowing them to shape the rules within which they would be judged.

label: Commission constantly delayed process by reopening resolved issues
original_label: Commission constantly delayed process by reopening resolved issues
quote: The Commission should have acted to mitigate the central role played by the overrepresented industry representatives in the work of the RDE-LDV working group, who constantly delayed its work by re-opening topics that were considered clarified or even decided upon.
context: The committee found that industry representatives within the working groups deliberately obstructed progress on more stringent testing, exemplifying how pressure was transmitted through institutional channels.

label: Manufacturers optimized only for laboratory test conditions
original_label: Manufacturers optimized only for laboratory test conditions
quote: The optimisation strategies put in place by car manufacturers specifically to meet the emission limits during the NEDC.
context: The report documents that manufacturers calibrated vehicles to pass laboratory tests but not to meet real-world conditions, indicating a deliberate choice to meet testing requirements rather than the underlying regulatory goal.

label: Manufacturers switch off emissions controls outside test temperature ranges
original_label: Manufacturers switch off emissions controls outside test temperature ranges
quote: Some manufacturers calibrate ECUs to decrease the effectiveness of ECTs outside specific 'thermal windows' that are close to the ambient temperature range prescribed by the NEDC, for instance by switching off emission control systems at ambient temperatures below 17 °C, while others are able to keep ECTs effective in much larger temperature ranges
context: The report identifies a specific defeat strategy: manufacturers deliberately deactivated working emissions controls outside narrow temperature bands, showing they possessed the technology but chose not to deploy it.

label: Thermal windows narrower than technically necessary
original_label: Thermal windows narrower than technically necessary
quote: Those thermal windows are rarely justifiable according to the technical limitations of the ECTs.
context: Technical experts concluded that the narrow temperature ranges were commercial choices, not engineering necessities, proving manufacturers knew they were choosing suboptimal emissions control.

label: Manufacturers modulate emissions control based on test duration
original_label: Manufacturers modulate emissions control based on test duration
quote: Others modulate ECTs to decrease their efficiency after a certain time from the start of the engine, close to the duration of the test, has elapsed. Moreover, in many cases, emissions measured on a test cycle after a certain period following engine start are unjustifiably higher, given the technical functionality of ECTs, than on the same cycle with measurements done immediately after engine start.
context: The report documents that manufacturers programmed emissions controls to degrade at test-cycle duration, a strategy with no legitimate engineering purpose other than passing the specific test.

label: Commercial objectives drove emissions control strategy choices
original_label: Commercial objectives drove emissions control strategy choices
quote: Optimisation strategies that reduce the effectiveness of ECTs can be attributed to commercial choices made by the car manufacturer to achieve different objectives, such as reducing fuel consumption, increasing user convenience, reducing costs by using cheaper parts or addressing design constraints. These objectives are not covered by the exemptions on the prohibition on the use of defeat devices.
context: The committee explicitly found that manufacturers chose to degrade emissions controls to save money and improve user convenience, not for technical reasons covered by regulatory exemptions.

label: Industry expected to meet Euro 6 NOx limits by 2014-2015
original_label: Industry expected to meet Euro 6 NOx limits by 2014-2015
quote: As a result of certain Member States favouring a higher value for the conformity factor, new car models will not have to respect until 2020 the not-to-exceed Euro 6 emission standards, already agreed by the co-legislators in 2007. This is six years later than originally planned and three years later with respect to the timing proposed in the Commission CARS 2020 communication of 8 November 2012 (COM(2012)0636).
context: The report shows that manufacturers faced a mandate to meet 80 mg/km NOx limits in real driving by 2014-2015, creating a technical and commercial challenge that drove the choice of defeat strategies.

label: Persistent NOx exceedances hindered air quality improvements
original_label: Persistent NOx exceedances hindered air quality improvements
quote: The persistent exceedances of NOx emissions by the automotive sector, coupled with the increased share of diesel cars in the EU fleet, hindered rapid reduction of NOx (and in particular NO2) concentrations in cities, despite the 58 % overall reduction in NOx emissions since 1990 in the EU
context: The report notes that despite overall progress, the vehicle sector failed to deliver expected NOx reductions, indicating that the industry's performance fell short of what the technology allowed.

label: NEDC test inadequate but no alternative available until 2017
original_label: NEDC test inadequate but no alternative available until 2017
quote: the inadequacy of the NEDC laboratory test, which is not representative of real-world emissions, and to the optimisation strategies put in place by car manufacturers to pass the laboratory test by calibrating vehicles' ECTs so that their effectiveness is only ensured within the boundary conditions of the NEDC test.
context: The report documents that all manufacturers faced the same constraint: a fundamentally inadequate test procedure with no compliant alternative until 2017, forcing a choice between the test and reality.

label: Commission deprioritized RDE development after 2008 financial crisis
original_label: Commission deprioritized RDE development after 2008 financial crisis
quote: The excessive length of the process leading to the introduction of regulatory RDE tests cannot be sufficiently explained only by the complexity of the development of a new test procedure, the time needed for the technological development of PEMS, and the length of the decision-making and administrative processes at EU level. The delays were also due to choices of political priorities, lobby influence and constant pressure from the industry that directed the focus of the Commission and the Member States to avoiding burdens on industry in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis.
context: The inquiry concluded that after 2008, Commission and Member State leadership intentionally delayed tighter testing to avoid imposing compliance costs on manufacturers, signaling that regulatory relief was a priority.

label: US EPA discovered defeat devices; EU market under no comparable pressure
original_label: US EPA discovered defeat devices; EU market under no comparable pressure
quote: Despite the risk of the possible use of defeat devices was generally known for light-duty and heavy-duty vehicles... it seems that generally it was not suspected that defeat devices could be in actual use in any passenger car produced in the EU until Volkswagen admitted to having used defeat software in its diesel cars sold on the US market
context: The stark difference in outcomes between the US (where EPA actively investigated) and EU (where no one investigated) shows that competitive and enforcement pressure in the US drove VW's exposure, while the EU market lacked equivalent pressure.

label: Conformity factor allows 168 mg/km instead of 80 mg/km
original_label: Conformity factor allows 168 mg/km instead of 80 mg/km
quote: The RDE test endorsed by the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) on 28 October 2015 introduced a 'temporary conformity factor' of 2.1 with the effect of allowing vehicles to emit 168 mg/km of NOx in the RDE test, applicable to all new vehicles as of September 2019 (and to new vehicle types as of September 2017), i.e. four years after the entry into force of the 80 mg/km limit value under the Euro 6 rules.
context: The committee documents how industry pressure induced a conformity factor that effectively doubled the regulatory target for four years, institutionalizing the legitimacy of suboptimal performance.

label: No type-approval authority tested beyond NEDC before 2015
original_label: No type-approval authority tested beyond NEDC before 2015
quote: No EU or Member State authority searched for defeat devices or proved the illegal use of defeat devices before September 2015. No Member State authority or technical service performed any tests other than the NEDC in the scope of type-approval, which in itself cannot point to the use of a defeat device.
context: The inquiry found that despite decades of awareness of NOx exceedances, no authority conducted alternative tests that would have exposed the strategies, indicating a collective choice not to investigate.

label: Manufacturers interpreted testing as only legal requirement
original_label: Manufacturers interpreted testing as only legal requirement
quote: In their answers to the questionnaire sent by the committee, all car manufacturers stated that they used these exceptions
context: Manufacturers framed compliance with narrow test conditions as sufficient legal compliance, downgrading the actual regulatory requirement to meet limits in normal use.

label: Member States delayed RDE adoption to avoid industry burden
original_label: Member States delayed RDE adoption to avoid industry burden
quote: The analysis of the minutes of the RDE-LDV working group and of the TCMV shows that some Member States acted on several occasions to delay the adoption process of the RDE tests and to favour less stringent testing methods. In addition, several Member States (Italy, Spain, France, the Slovak Republic, Romania and Hungary) prevented the formation of a qualified majority in the TCMV, resulting in a postponement of the vote on the first RDE package
context: The inquiry documents that Member States deliberately obstructed tighter testing standards, transmitting industry pressure upward to institutional level, delaying real-world testing by years.

label: Manufacturers stated they used thermal window derogations
original_label: Manufacturers stated they used thermal window derogations
quote: In fact, often the choice of the emission control strategies employed by some manufacturers seems driven only by the goal of passing the test, which they interpreted as the only legal requirement to be fulfilled in spite of the clear air quality objectives of the legislation
context: Manufacturers explicitly defined their goal as passing the test rather than meeting the underlying air quality requirement, showing a strategic narrowing of compliance scope.

label: Euro 5 limits achievable with available technology at time
original_label: Euro 5 limits achievable with available technology at time
quote: Emission control technologies (ECTs) available at the time of adoption of the Euro 5 and 6 NOx emission limits, when properly applied, already allowed diesel cars to meet the Euro 5 NOx emission limit of 180 mg/km and the Euro 6 NOx emission limit of 80 mg/km by the date of their respective entry into force, in real world conditions and not only in laboratory tests.
context: The committee's expert consensus was that compliant technology existed at the time Euro standards were set, meaning legitimate means were available but manufacturers chose not to use them.

label: Diesel technology crucial to competing on CO2 targets
original_label: Diesel technology crucial to competing on CO2 targets
quote: whereas this sustained growth in market share of diesel vehicles also came about as a result of EU climate policy, as diesel technology has an advantage over petrol engines when it comes to CO2 emissions
context: The report establishes that manufacturers needed diesel to compete on mandated CO2 targets, creating structural pressure that made abandoning or modifying diesel unacceptable.

label: Commission failed to escalate RDE process to Council level
original_label: Commission failed to escalate RDE process to Council level
quote: Despite the issue of pollutant emissions from vehicles being not only a highly sensitive and political issue, but also a subject of great concern to EU citizens, the Commission did not make any attempt to advance the decision-making process by making use of the possibility envisaged in the Regulatory Procedure with Scrutiny to bring the proposal to the level of the Council in order to increase political awareness and to exercise additional pressure on obstructing Member States.
context: The inquiry found that the Commission deliberately chose not to escalate pressure against Member States and manufacturers who were blocking tighter testing requirements.

label: No requirement to disclose emission control strategies until 2016
original_label: No requirement to disclose emission control strategies until 2016
quote: Before the adoption of the 2nd RDE package, car manufacturers were not required to declare or justify their emission strategies (except at specified low temperatures): notably, the requirement to disclose the 'auxiliary emission strategies', which change the base strategies for a specific purpose and in response to a specific set of ambient or operating conditions, was not provided for in the legislation until April 2016
context: The regulatory framework did not require manufacturers to disclose or justify emissions strategies, removing a key control mechanism that would have exposed the defeat strategies.

label: Volkswagen installed software to detect and adjust for testing
original_label: Volkswagen installed software to detect and adjust for testing
quote: The notice alleged that the group installed software on certain diesel vehicles to detect when the vehicle is undergoing emissions testing, and that the software turns on full emissions controls only during the test but reduces their effectiveness during normal driving.
context: VW made an explicit choice to install test-detection software that enabled emissions control modulation, a deliberate deviation from legitimate means of compliance.

label: DG ENV warned DG ENTR of inadequate RDE timeline
original_label: DG ENV warned DG ENTR of inadequate RDE timeline
quote: In January 2013 the Danish Minister for the Environment, Ida Auken, wrote to the then Commissioners Tajani and Potočnik raising concerns as to the possibility for Denmark and many other Member States to reach NO2 air quality targets in view of emissions from light duty vehicles, considering the RDE timeline 'unacceptable' and asking for action on the 'critical situation as soon as possible'.
context: External pressure from environmental authorities signaled that the RDE timeline was inadequate, but this pressure did not accelerate the process, indicating organizational resistance to tightening standards.

label: Real-world NOx emissions 2-14 times laboratory limits
original_label: Real-world NOx emissions 2-14 times laboratory limits
quote: There are large discrepancies between the NOx emissions of most Euro 3-6 diesel cars measured during the type-approval process with the New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) laboratory test, which meet the legal emission limit, and their NOx emissions measured in real driving conditions, which substantially exceed the limit.
context: The report documents the core performance gap: vehicles passed laboratory tests by 2-14x margins but failed in real driving, showing systemic failure of the entire testing regime.

label: EGR systems face technical challenges at low temperatures
original_label: EGR systems face technical challenges at low temperatures
quote: Driving at very low ambient temperatures (or at very high altitudes where air pressure is low), can pose a challenge for EGR systems, due to the possible creation of soot, hydrocarbons and condensates that may clog the EGR valve or intercooler, and cause, for instance, increased PM or hydrocarbon pollutant emissions
context: The report acknowledges genuine technical constraints but then documents that manufacturers used unnecessarily narrow thermal windows, showing they chose not to solve the engineering challenge.

label: Manufacturers could expand temperature ranges but chose not to
original_label: Manufacturers could expand temperature ranges but chose not to
quote: Following the Volkswagen scandal, some car manufacturers have adjusted their thermal windows to allow their existing emissions control technologies to operate within a much broader temperature range.
context: The post-scandal behavior proves that manufacturers possessed the technical capability to operate across broader ranges all along but had chosen not to, confirming the deviation was a choice.

label: US markets diesel cars at 44 mg/km NOx; EU at 80 mg/km
original_label: US markets diesel cars at 44 mg/km NOx; EU at 80 mg/km
quote: A lower NOx emission limit of 44 mg/km was already in place in the US at the time of the introduction of Euro 5 limits
context: The regulatory gap shows manufacturers faced a dual-goal pressure: meet stricter US limits for US sales while selling compliant-but-worse EU vehicles in Europe, creating incentive to exploit the EU's weaker standard.

label: Heavy-duty emissions scandals in 1990s set precedent
original_label: Heavy-duty emissions scandals in 1990s set precedent
quote: Defeat devices were found in the US in light-duty vehicles in 1995 and in heavy-duty vehicles in 1998
context: The prior discovery of heavy-duty defeat devices in the 1990s, despite being known in the industry, failed to trigger EU preventive measures, showing the market was de facto permissive toward such strategies.

label: Member States presented different positions publicly versus internally
original_label: Member States presented different positions publicly versus internally
quote: Some Member States presented a different position to the public from that they presented to the participants of the TCMV.
context: The committee found evidence that Member States duplicitously supported tighter standards in public while secretly obstructing them in technical committees, showing hierarchical pressure to hide pro-industry stances.

label: Full RDE procedure not adopted until 2016; manufacturers needed interim compliance
original_label: Full RDE procedure not adopted until 2016; manufacturers needed interim compliance
quote: The work on the second RDE package, setting out the not-to-exceed limits for NOx emissions, started in February 2015 and accelerated after the Volkswagen revelations in September 2015 The second package was adopted by the TCMV on 28 October 2015.
context: Real-world testing was not finalized until late 2015 even though the NOx standard entered force in 2014-2015, leaving manufacturers with no legitimate real-world standard to meet during the critical transition period.

label: Commissioner Tajani explained RDE would apply 'at latest from 2017'
original_label: Commissioner Tajani explained RDE would apply 'at latest from 2017'
quote: In his answer of 26 March 2013 Mr Tajani explained that the Commission had initiated as early as 2011 the RDE procedure to bring about a robust procedure test, which would apply at the latest from 2017.
context: Senior Commission leadership telegraphed to concerned Member States that RDE would not arrive until 2017, three years after Euro 6 entry, de facto signaling that interim non-compliance was acceptable.

label: US diesel market entry as strategic priority
original_label: US diesel market entry as strategic priority
quote: In or about at least 2006, VW employees working under the supervision of DORENKAMP and HADLER were designing the new EA 189 2.0 liter diesel engine (later known as the Generation 1 or "Gen 1") that would be the cornerstone of a new project to sell passenger diesel vehicles in the United States. Selling diesel vehicles in the U.S. market was an important strategic goal of VW AG. This project became known within VW as the "US'07'' project.
context: The indictment establishes VW's explicit strategic goal to enter and sell diesel vehicles in the US market through the US'07 project beginning in 2006.

label: Technical infeasibility of meeting NOx standards and customer demand simultaneously
original_label: Technical infeasibility of meeting NOx standards and customer demand simultaneously
quote: DORENKAMP, HADLER, and their co-conspirators, however, realized that they could not design a diesel engine that would both meet the stricter NOx emissions standards that would become effective in 2007 and attract sufficient customer demand in the U.S. market.
context: The indictment documents the key moment where VW engineers acknowledged that the legitimate path—designing a compliant engine that also met market demand—was not feasible.

label: Decision to install defeat device instead of legitimate compliance
original_label: Decision to install defeat device instead of legitimate compliance
quote: Instead of bringing to market a diesel vehicle that could legitimately meet the new, more restrictive U.S. NOx emissions standards, VW employees acting at the direction of DORENKAMP, HADLER, and their co-conspirators, designed, created, and implemented a software function (the "defeat device") to cheat the standard U.S. emissions tests. DORENKAMP, HADLER, and their co-conspirators referred to the software as, among other things, the "acoustic function," "switch logic," "cycle beating," or "emissions-tight mode."
context: The indictment establishes the moment of choice: faced with technical infeasibility, VW leadership chose to install cheating software rather than pursue legitimate compliance.

label: Design of software to detect and evade emissions testing
original_label: Design of software to detect and evade emissions testing
quote: While employees acting at their direction designed and implemented the defeat device software, DORENKAMP, HADLER, and their co-conspirators knew that U.S. regulators would measure VW's diesel vehicles' emissions through standard tests with specific, published drive cycles. VW employees acting at the direction of DORENKAMP, HADLER, and their co-conspirators designed the VW defeat device to recognize whether the vehicle was undergoing standard U.S. emissions testing on a dynamometer (or "dyno") or whether the vehicle was being driven on the road under normal driving conditions. The defeat device accomplished this by recognizing the standard drive cycles used by U.S. regulators. If the vehicle's software detected that it was being tested, the vehicle performed in one mode, which satisfied U.S. NOx emissions standards. If the vehicle's software detected that the vehicle was not being tested, it operated in a different mode, in which the effectiveness of the vehicle's emissions control systems was reduced substantially, causing the vehicle to emit substantially higher NOx, sometimes 35 times higher than allowable U.S. standards.
context: The indictment describes how VW deliberately engineered the defeat device software to detect test conditions and operate in dual modes—compliant during testing, non-compliant during normal driving.

label: Dorenkamp authorizes defeat device despite employee concerns
original_label: Dorenkamp authorizes defeat device despite employee concerns
quote: Throughout in or around 2006, DORENKAMP authorized VW engineers to use the defeat device in the development of the US'07 project, despite concerns expressed by certain VW AG employees about the propriety of designing and activating the defeat device software.
context: The indictment documents that DORENKAMP, as head of Engine Development, explicitly authorized the defeat device over the objections of subordinate engineers, showing hierarchical pressure to proceed with the illegal approach.

label: Hadler overrules technical objections and approves defeat device
original_label: Hadler overrules technical objections and approves defeat device

label: Dyno mode versus road mode emissions control

label: Off-balance-sheet treatment as management preference
original_label: Off-balance-sheet treatment as management preference

label: Hedging to reduce income volatility
original_label: Hedging to reduce income volatility

label: Merchant investments decline in late 2000 and early 2001

label: Raptor vehicles face negative credit capacity
original_label: Raptor vehicles face negative credit capacity
