label: Sales representatives trained to claim less than 1% addiction risk
original_label: Sales representatives trained to claim less than 1% addiction risk

label: Citing inadequate studies to support addiction safety claims
original_label: Citing inadequate studies to support addiction safety claims

label: OxyContin promotion despite comparable efficacy and safety to alternatives
original_label: OxyContin promotion despite comparable efficacy and safety to alternatives

label: Distributing branded promotional items unprecedented for Schedule II drug
original_label: Distributing branded promotional items unprecedented for Schedule II drug

label: Distributing OxyContin video without FDA prior approval or submission
original_label: Distributing OxyContin video without FDA prior approval or submission
quote: In 1998, Purdue distributed 15 000 copies of an OxyContin video to physicians without submitting it to the FDA for review, an oversight later acknowledged by Purdue. context: Van Zee documents Purdue's choice to distribute promotional material without regulatory approval and FDA later finding the material misrepresented risks and benefits.

label: Starter coupon program to initiate patient use
original_label: Starter coupon program to initiate patient use

label: OxyContin offered only dosing convenience, not clinical advantage
original_label: OxyContin offered only dosing convenience, not clinical advantage

original_label: Controversy over opioids for chronic non-cancer pain despite aggressive promotion

label: Targeting physician population without addiction expertise
original_label: Targeting physician population without addiction expertise

label: Using prescriber profiling to target high-volume opioid prescribers
original_label: Using prescriber profiling to target high-volume opioid prescribers

context: Van Zee explains how Purdue's use of prescriber profiling enabled targeting of the highest-volume opioid prescribers, including those who were 'least discriminate,' a choice that prioritized volume over appropriate clinical practice.

original_label: Misrepresenting addiction risk proved costly: $634M settlement

label: Mark-to-market accounting enables revenue acceleration
original_label: Mark-to-market accounting enables revenue acceleration

label: Accelerating income to meet quarterly targets
original_label: Accelerating income to meet quarterly targets

original_label: Enron's trading profits declining despite growing revenues

label: EES losses hidden through merger to appear profitable
original_label: EES losses hidden through merger to appear profitable

original_label: Mark-to-market valuation unreliable for long-term contracts

label: EES contracts could not be valued at claimed prices
original_label: EES contracts could not be valued at claimed prices

label: Enron's rapid growth and astonishing performance expectations
original_label: Enron's rapid growth and astonishing performance expectations

original_label: Enron stock price decline and analyst bullishness

original_label: Enron's dependence on continuous deal flow for earnings

original_label: Enron needed high stock price to fund trading operations

original_label: Enron used hedging transactions that were not true hedges

original_label: Enron used disguised loans as commodity trades

original_label: Enron needed consistent earnings growth to maintain valuation

original_label: Rating agencies embedded in capital markets with profit incentive

label: Credit raters have no incentive to catch wrongdoers
original_label: Credit raters have no incentive to catch wrongdoers
quote: The problem is that the credit rating agencies have no incentive to catch the few wrongdoers, no matter how huge the consequences to the market. Duke Law School Professor Steven Schwarcz argued in his testimony at the Committee's March 20 hearing that reputational concerns are sufficient incentive for the credit rating agencies to be diligent in their work, and he cited their strong track record as proof. Assuming that most companies are honest, however, credit rating agencies will be correct in most cases without having to go much beyond the face of financial statements. Their limited liability and their entrenched position of power means that they do not have to go to additional lengths in order to expose the outlier corporations that are not being truthful.
context: Senate committee staff analyzing why credit rating agencies failed to detect Enron despite their market power and access.
